In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory,﴾ ﴿that God may forgive you your sins, past and future, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path,﴾ ﴿and that God may help you with a mighty help.﴾

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory,﴾ ﴿that God may forgive you your sins, past and future, complete His favor upon you, and guide you to a straight path,﴾ ﴿and that God may help you with a mighty help.﴾ And in it are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding al-Fath (the victory/opening), there are several views:

The first: it is the conquest of Makkah, which is evident.

The second: the conquest of Rome and others.

The third: what is meant by al-Fath is the Treaty of al-Hudaybiyyah (sulh al-Hudaybiyah).

The fourth: the opening of Islam through proof and demonstration, and through the sword and the spear.

The fifth: what is meant is judgment (hukm), as in His saying: ﴿Our Lord, decide between us and our people with truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89], and His saying: ﴿Then will your Lord judge between us with truth﴾ [Saba': 26]. The preferred view among all of these is several meanings:

The first: the conquest of Makkah.

The second: the conquest of al-Hudaybiyyah.

The third: the opening of Islam through signs, clarification, proof and demonstration.

The first is appropriate to the end of what precedes it, in several respects:

The first: when He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Here you are, those who are invited to spend in the way of God﴾ [Muhammad: 38], up to His saying: ﴿And whoever is stingy, is only stingy against himself﴾ [Muhammad: 38], He made clear that He gave them the conquest of Makkah, they seized their homes, and they obtained many times what they had spent; and had they been stingy, that would have been lost to them, so their stinginess would only be against themselves.

The second: when He said: ﴿And God is with you﴾ [Muhammad: 35] and said: ﴿And you will be the superior ones﴾ [Muhammad: 35], He demonstrated His proof through the conquest of Makkah, for they were the superior ones.

The third: when God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So do not weaken and call for peace﴾ [Muhammad: 35], and its meaning was: do not ask for reconciliation from your own side, but be patient, for they will ask for reconciliation and strive for it, as happened on the day of al-Hudaybiyyah, which is the intended meaning of al-Fath in one of the views, and as the conquest of Makkah was when the chieftains of Quraysh came seeking safety, as believers and as Muslims. If it is said: if the intended meaning is the conquest of Makkah, then Makkah had not yet been conquered, so how did He say ﴿We have given you a clear victory﴾ in the past tense? We say: the answer to this is in two respects:

The first: "We have opened" in Our judgment and Our decree. The second: what
[Page 68]
God has decreed is certain to occur, so He reported it in the past tense to indicate that it is a matter that none can repel and an event that none can prevent.

The second issue: His saying: ﴿that God may forgive you﴾ indicates that the conquest is a cause of forgiveness, yet conquest is not fit to be a cause of forgiveness. What is the answer to this? We say: the answer to this is in several respects:

The first: what has been said is that He did not make the conquest a cause of forgiveness alone, but it is a cause for the gathering of the matters mentioned, namely: forgiveness, the completion of favor, guidance and victory, as if He, exalted is He, said: "that God may forgive you, complete His favor, guide you and help you." Undoubtedly this gathering was only established through the conquest, for favor was completed by it, and victory became general after it.

The second: that the conquest of Makkah was a cause for the purification of the House of God, exalted is He, from the filth of idols, and the purification of His House became a cause for the purification of His servant.

The third: that through the conquest the Hajj is achieved, and through the Hajj forgiveness is achieved. Do you not see the supplication of the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, when he said regarding the Hajj: "O God, make it an accepted Hajj, a striving that is thanked, and a sin that is forgiven."

The fourth: what is meant by it is recognition. Its meaning: ﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾ so that it may be known that you are forgiven and protected, for people had known after the Year of the Elephant that Makkah would not be taken by the enemy of God, who is cursed, and that only the beloved of God, the one forgiven, would enter it and take it.

The third issue: The Prophet ﷺ had no sin, so what is forgiven for him? We say: the answer to this has been mentioned many times before, in several respects:

The first: what is meant is the sin of the believers.

The second: what is meant is leaving what is more excellent.

The third: minor sins, for they are permissible for the prophets through forgetfulness and deliberate action, and He protects them from vanity.

The fourth: what is meant is infallibility (al-'ismah), and we have explained its basis in the Surah of Muhammad.

The fourth issue: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿what has been delayed﴾? We say there are several views:

The first: that He promised the Prophet, upon him be peace, that he would not sin after prophethood.

The second: what preceded the conquest and what followed the conquest.

The third: generality. It is said: "Strike whoever you meet and whoever you do not meet," although one who is not met cannot be struck, as an indication of generality.

The fourth: before prophethood and after it. On this view, what preceded prophethood is by pardon, and what followed it by infallibility. There are other views, which are weak, among them the saying of some: what preceded is the matter of Mariyah, and what followed is the matter of Zaynab. This is the most distant and weakest of views, for the speech does not cohere.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and complete His favor upon you﴾ may have several meanings:

The first: that the obligations were completed at the conquest, since the Hajj became obligatory, and it is the last of the obligations, and obligations are favors.

The second: He completes His favor upon you by clearing the land for you of your opponents, for on the day of the conquest there remained for the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, no enemy of any standing, for some of them had been destroyed at Badr, and the rest believed and sought safety on the day of the conquest.

The third: and He completes His favor upon you in this world by answering your supplication in seeking the conquest, and in the Hereafter by granting your intercession for sins, even if they are of the utmost ugliness. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ may have several meanings: (the most apparent of them): He keeps you upon the straight path so that no one remains who would turn to his words from the misguided, or from those who could compel (others) to disbelief. This agrees with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], in that I destroyed those who disputed about it and brought them to faith.

The second: it may be said that He made the conquest a cause for guidance to the straight path, because it facilitated jihad for the believers, given their knowledge of the immediate benefits through the conquest and the deferred ones through the promise. Jihad is the traveling of the way of God, and for this reason the one who fights in the way of God is called a mujahid.

The third: what we mentioned, that the intended meaning is recognition, i.e., so that it may be known that you are upon a straight path, in that the conquest does not occur except at the hand of one who is upon the path of God, as evidenced by the story of the Elephant. His saying: ﴿and that God may help you with a mighty help﴾ is clear, for through the conquest the victory became manifest and the matter became famous.

Here there are two issues, one linguistic and the other semantic:

[Page 69]
As for the linguistic issue: God described the victory as "mighty" (ʿazīz), and the mighty is one who possesses victory. (The answer): in two respects:

The first: what al-Zamakhshari said, that it may have three meanings:

The first: its meaning is: it was helped when it was mighty, like His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning: possessing pleasure.

The second: describing the victory with what the one helped is described with, as a metaphorical attribution, as one says: "He has a truthful speech," just as one says: "He is truthful."

The third: describing the victory as "mighty," its possessor being mighty.

The second answer is that we say: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned of these estimations is only binding on us if we say that "might" derives from overpowering, and the mighty is the overpowering. But if we say that the mighty is the precious, the rare in its like, or the one needed yet rare in existence, as one says "the thing became rare" when its existence is scarce while it is needed, then the victory was needed, and the like of it was not found, namely taking the House of God from the unbelievers who were entrenched in it without any count.

As for the semantic issue: when God, exalted is He, said: ﴿that God may forgive you your sins past﴾, He made the Agent explicit, which is God, and then conjoined to it with His saying: ﴿and complete﴾ and with His saying: ﴿and guide you﴾, and He did not mention the word "God" in the fine manner of speech, which is that when many acts proceed from one agent, his name appears in the first act and does not appear in what follows it. You say: "Zayd came, spoke, stood and departed," and you do not say: "Zayd came and Zayd sat," for brevity by restricting oneself to the first. Here He did not say "and help you with help," but repeated the word "God." We say this is guidance to the way of victory. For this reason God has rarely mentioned victory without attribution. He said: ﴿by the victory of God He gives victory﴾ [al-Rum: 5], and did not say "by victory He gives victory." He said: ﴿It is He who supported you with His victory﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and did not say "with victory." He said: ﴿When the victory of God and the opening come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], and He said: ﴿A victory from God and a near opening﴾, and did not say "a victory and an opening." He said: ﴿And victory is only from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 126]. This is the most conclusive of the verses for our claim. Its verification is that victory is through patience, and patience is through God, as He said: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is only through God﴾ [al-Nahl: 127]. This is because patience is the tranquility and calm of the heart, and that comes through the remembrance of God, as He said: ﴿Verily, by the remembrance of God hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. So when He said here "and God help you," He made the word "God" explicit as a reminder for teaching that through the remembrance of God the hearts attain tranquility, through it patience is attained, and through it victory is realized.

Here is another issue: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have opened﴾, then said: ﴿that God may forgive you﴾, and He did not say "Indeed, We have opened so that We may forgive you," to magnify the matter of the conquest. This is because forgiveness, although great, is general, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and He said: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. And if we say that what is meant by forgiveness regarding the Prophet, upon him be peace, is infallibility, that was not specific to our Prophet, for other messengers were also infallible. Completing the favor is similarly so; God said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favor upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and He said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. Likewise guidance: God said: ﴿and guides to Himself whoever turns penitently﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], generalizing it. Likewise victory: God said: ﴿And already has Our word preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they are the ones who will be helped﴾ [al-Saffat: 171–172]. As for the conquest, it was not for anyone other than the Prophet ﷺ, so He magnified it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory﴾. In this there is magnification in two respects: the first is "Indeed, We"; the second is "for you," i.e., for your sake, in the manner of a favor.

Its meaning: ﴿Indeed, We have given you﴾ so that it may be known that you are forgiven and protected, for people had known after the Year of the Elephant that Makkah would not be taken by the enemy of God, who is cursed, and that only the beloved of God, the one forgiven, would enter it and take it.

The third issue: The Prophet ﷺ had no sin, so what is forgiven for him? We say: the answer to this has been mentioned many times before, in several respects:

The first: what is meant is the sin of the believers.

The second: what is meant is leaving what is more excellent.

The third: minor sins, for they are permissible for the prophets through forgetfulness and deliberate action, and He protects them from vanity.

The fourth: what is meant is infallibility (al-'ismah), and we have explained its basis in the Surah of Muhammad.

The fourth issue: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿what has been delayed﴾? We say there are several views:

The first: that He promised the Prophet, upon him be peace, that he would not sin after prophethood.

The second: what preceded the conquest and what followed the conquest.

The third: generality. It is said: "Strike whoever you meet and whoever you do not meet," although one who is not met cannot be struck, as an indication of generality.

The fourth: before prophethood and after it. On this view, what preceded prophethood is by pardon, and what followed it by infallibility. There are other views, which are weak, among them the saying of some: what preceded is the matter of Mariyah, and what followed is the matter of Zaynab. This is the most distant and weakest of views, for the speech does not cohere.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and complete His favor upon you﴾ may have several meanings:

The first: that the obligations were completed at the conquest, since the Hajj became obligatory, and it is the last of the obligations, and obligations are favors.

The second: He completes His favor upon you by clearing the land for you of your opponents, for on the day of the conquest there remained for the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, no enemy of any standing, for some of them had been destroyed at Badr, and the rest believed and sought safety on the day of the conquest.

The third: and He completes His favor upon you in this world by answering your supplication in seeking the conquest, and in the Hereafter by granting your intercession for sins, even if they are of the utmost ugliness. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and guide you to a straight path﴾ may have several meanings: (the most apparent of them): He keeps you upon the straight path so that no one remains who would turn to his words from the misguided, or from those who could compel (others) to disbelief. This agrees with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I have approved Islam as a religion for you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], in that I destroyed those who disputed about it and brought them to faith.

The second: it may be said that He made the conquest a cause for guidance to the straight path, because it facilitated jihad for the believers, given their knowledge of the immediate benefits through the conquest and the deferred ones through the promise. Jihad is the traveling of the way of God, and for this reason the one who fights in the way of God is called a mujahid.

The third: what we mentioned, that the intended meaning is recognition, i.e., so that it may be known that you are upon a straight path, in that the conquest does not occur except at the hand of one who is upon the path of God, as evidenced by the story of the Elephant. His saying: ﴿and that God may help you with a mighty help﴾ is clear, for through the conquest the victory became manifest and the matter became famous.

Here there are two issues, one linguistic and the other semantic:

[Page 69]
As for the linguistic issue: God described the victory as "mighty" (ʿazīz), and the mighty is one who possesses victory. (The answer): in two respects:

The first: what al-Zamakhshari said, that it may have three meanings:

The first: its meaning is: it was helped when it was mighty, like His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah: 21], meaning: possessing pleasure.

The second: describing the victory with what the one helped is described with, as a metaphorical attribution, as one says: "He has a truthful speech," just as one says: "He is truthful."

The third: describing the victory as "mighty," its possessor being mighty.

The second answer is that we say: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned of these estimations is only binding on us if we say that "might" derives from overpowering, and the mighty is the overpowering. But if we say that the mighty is the precious, the rare in its like, or the one needed yet rare in existence, as one says "the thing became rare" when its existence is scarce while it is needed, then the victory was needed, and the like of it was not found, namely taking the House of God from the unbelievers who were entrenched in it without any count.

As for the semantic issue: when God, exalted is He, said: ﴿that God may forgive you your sins past﴾, He made the Agent explicit, which is God, and then conjoined to it with His saying: ﴿and complete﴾ and with His saying: ﴿and guide you﴾, and He did not mention the word "God" in the fine manner of speech, which is that when many acts proceed from one agent, his name appears in the first act and does not appear in what follows it. You say: "Zayd came, spoke, stood and departed," and you do not say: "Zayd came and Zayd sat," for brevity by restricting oneself to the first. Here He did not say "and help you with help," but repeated the word "God." We say this is guidance to the way of victory. For this reason God has rarely mentioned victory without attribution. He said: ﴿by the victory of God He gives victory﴾ [al-Rum: 5], and did not say "by victory He gives victory." He said: ﴿It is He who supported you with His victory﴾ [al-Anfal: 62], and did not say "with victory." He said: ﴿When the victory of God and the opening come﴾ [al-Nasr: 1], and He said: ﴿A victory from God and a near opening﴾, and did not say "a victory and an opening." He said: ﴿And victory is only from God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 126]. This is the most conclusive of the verses for our claim. Its verification is that victory is through patience, and patience is through God, as He said: ﴿And be patient, and your patience is only through God﴾ [al-Nahl: 127]. This is because patience is the tranquility and calm of the heart, and that comes through the remembrance of God, as He said: ﴿Verily, by the remembrance of God hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28]. So when He said here "and God help you," He made the word "God" explicit as a reminder for teaching that through the remembrance of God the hearts attain tranquility, through it patience is attained, and through it victory is realized.

Here is another issue: God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have opened﴾, then said: ﴿that God may forgive you﴾, and He did not say "Indeed, We have opened so that We may forgive you," to magnify the matter of the conquest. This is because forgiveness, although great, is general, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, God forgives all sins﴾ [al-Zumar: 53], and He said: ﴿and He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. And if we say that what is meant by forgiveness regarding the Prophet, upon him be peace, is infallibility, that was not specific to our Prophet, for other messengers were also infallible. Completing the favor is similarly so; God said: ﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favor upon you﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3], and He said: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favor which I bestowed upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 40]. Likewise guidance: God said: ﴿and guides to Himself whoever turns penitently﴾ [al-Ra'd: 27], generalizing it. Likewise victory: God said: ﴿And already has Our word preceded for Our servants, the messengers. Indeed, they are the ones who will be helped﴾ [al-Saffat: 171–172]. As for the conquest, it was not for anyone other than the Prophet ﷺ, so He magnified it by His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have given you a clear victory﴾. In this there is magnification in two respects: the first is "Indeed, We"; the second is "for you," i.e., for your sake, in the manner of a favor.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility (al-sakinah) into the hearts of the believers, that they might increase in faith along with their faith. And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Knowing, Wise.﴾

When Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿and Allah would help you﴾, He explained the manner of the help. This is because Allah, exalted is He, may help His messengers with a cry by which He destroys their enemies, or with a quake that decrees their annihilation, or with an army He sends down from the sky, or with help, strength and steadfastness of heart which He bestows upon the believers, so that they may thereby have a great reward. So He said: ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility﴾, meaning, as a confirmation of the help. Regarding tranquility (al-sakinah) there are several meanings:

The first: it is calm (al-sukun).

The second: dignity (al-waqar) toward Allah and His Messenger, which derives from calm.

The third: certainty (al-yaqin). All of them derive from calm. On this there are the following issues:

The first issue: the tranquility mentioned here is other than the tranquility in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the sign of His kingdom is that there will come to you the chest (al-tabut) in which is tranquility from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 248], according to the view of most of the exegetes. It is possible that it is that same one, and what is intended by it, according to all the meanings, is certainty and steadfastness of hearts.

The second issue: the tranquility sent down upon them is the cause of their remembrance of Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Verily, by the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest﴾ [al-Ra'd: 28].

The third issue: Allah, exalted is He, said concerning the disbelievers: ﴿And He cast fear into their hearts﴾ [al-Ahzab: 26], using the word "casting" (al-qadhf), which is disturbing, and He said concerning the believers: ﴿He sent down tranquility﴾, using the word "sending down" (al-inzal), which is affirming. In this there is a legal meaning: whoever knows something beforehand, remembers it, and continually keeps it in mind, will not be shaken when it occurs; whereas whoever was heedless of something and it befalls him suddenly, his heart trembles. Do you not see that one who is informed of the occurrence of a cry and is told, "Do not be alarmed by it," does not tremble when the cry occurs; whereas one who is not informed of it, or was informed but forgot it, trembles when it occurs. Likewise, the disbeliever, Allah comes upon him from where he does not expect, and casts into his heart, so he trembles; while the believer, Allah comes upon him from where he had been remembering, so he is calmed.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾, there are several meanings:

The first: He commanded them with obligations one after another, and they believed in each of them. For example, they were commanded with monotheism, and they believed and obeyed; then they were commanded with fighting and pilgrimage, and they believed and obeyed. Thus they increased in faith along with their faith.

The second: He sent down tranquility upon them, so they were patient, and they saw with the eye of certainty what they had known with the knowledge of certainty about the help. Thus they had faith derived from witnessing (al-shahadah) along with their faith derived from the unseen (al-ghayb). So they increased in faith derived from witnessing along with their faith derived from the unseen.

The third: they increased in the branches (al-furu') along with their belief in the roots (al-usul). For they believed that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, that Allah is One, and that the Gathering (al-hashr) will take place; and they believed that everything the Prophet (ﷺ) says is true, and that everything Allah, exalted is He, commands is obligatory.

The fourth: they increased in inferential faith (al-iman al-istidlali) along with their innate faith (al-iman al-fitri). On this aspect we point out a subtle point: Allah, exalted is He, said concerning the disbeliever: ﴿We only give them respite that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178], and He did not say "along with their disbelief," because their disbelief is obstinate (inadi), and there is no innate disbelief in existence for obstinate disbelief to be joined to; rather, disbelief is nothing but obstinate. Likewise, one does not say that disbelief in the branches was joined to disbelief in the roots, because it is necessary for disbelief in the roots to entail disbelief in the branches; whereas it is not necessary for belief in the roots to entail belief in the branches in the sense of obedience and submission. Hence He said: ﴿that they might increase in faith along with their faith﴾.

His saying: ﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾. He was able to destroy His enemy with His soldiers, indeed with a cry, but He did not do so; rather He sent down tranquility upon the believers, so that the destruction of their enemies would be by their own hands, and thus they would have the reward. Regarding the soldiers of the heavens and the earth there are several meanings:

The first: the angels of the heavens and the earth.

The second: the angels in the heavens and the animals and jinn on the earth.

The third: the heavenly and earthly causes, so that the falling of a fragment from the sky and the sinking of the earth are among His soldiers.

صفحة ٧١
As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and Allah is ever Knowing, Wise﴾: when He said, ﴿And to Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾, and their number is not limited, He affirmed knowledge, as an indication that ﴿not an atom's weight escapes Him in the heavens or on the earth﴾ [Saba': 3]. Also, when He mentioned the matter of the hearts with His saying ﴿It is He who sent down tranquility into the hearts of the believers﴾, and faith is an act of the hearts, He mentioned knowledge as an indication that He knows the secret and what is more hidden. His saying "Wise" (hakim) after "Knowing" (alim) is an indication that He acts in accordance with knowledge, for the wise is one who does a thing with perfection and knows it. Whoever produces a wondrous work by coincidence is not called wise, and whoever knows and acts contrary to knowledge is not called wise.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 48, verse 5:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿That He may admit the believing men and the believing women into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and remove from them their misdeeds. And that is with Allah a great attainment.﴾

It requires a preceding verb: ﴿li-yudkhila﴾ (that He may admit). For one who says at the outset, "li-tukrimanī" (that you may honour me), the speech is not sound unless he has first said "ji'tuka" (I came to you) or something that stands in its place. Regarding that verb there are several possibilities. Its states are controlled by saying: that verb is either explicitly mentioned or not mentioned, and in the latter case it should be understood. Then it is either understood from a verbal indicator that signifies it, or it is understood through a circumstantial indicator. If it is mentioned, it admits several possibilities:

The first: His saying ﴿li-yazdādū īmānan﴾ (that they may increase in faith). It is as if He, exalted is He, sent down tranquility so that they might increase in faith through the sending down, in order that He might admit them, through faith, into gardens. If it is said: His saying ﴿wa-yuʿadhdhiba﴾ (and punish) [al-Fath: 6] is conjoined to His saying ﴿li-yudkhila﴾, and the increase of their faith is not suitable as a cause for punishing them. We say: Yes, and that is from two aspects. The first of them: that the punishment is mentioned because it is an intended aim for the believers. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: Because of your increase in faith, He admits you in the Hereafter into gardens, and He punishes, through your hands in this world, the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

The second: its estimated form is "and He punishes because of what you have of increase," as one says: "I did it to test by it the enemy and the friend," meaning, to know by its existence the friend and by its absence the enemy. Thus, so that the believer may increase in faith and He admits him into Paradise, and the disbeliever may increase in disbelief and He punishes him thereby.

(Another aspect) third: that the cause of the increase in the faith of the believers is their abundant patience and steadfastness, so the hypocrite and the disbeliever are vexed by their presence and are tormented, and this is close to what we have mentioned.

The second: His saying ﴿wa-yanṣuraka Allāh﴾ (and Allah helps you). It is as if He, exalted is He, said: And Allah helps you through the believers, so that He may admit the believers into gardens.

The third: His saying ﴿li-yaghfira laka Allāh mā taqaddama min dhanbika﴾ (that Allah may forgive you what preceded of your sin). According to our view, the intended meaning is the sin of the believer. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: that He may forgive you the sin of the believers, so that He may admit the believers into gardens. As for if we say that it is understood from a non-explicit word, it also admits several possibilities. The first of them: His saying "ḥakīman" (Wise) indicates this. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: Allah is Wise; He did what He did so that He might admit the believers into gardens.

The second: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-yutimma niʿmatahu ʿalayk﴾ (and complete His favour upon you), in this world and the Hereafter, so He answers your supplication in this world and accepts your intercession in the next: ﴿li-yudkhila al-mu'minīna wa-al-mu'mināt jannāt﴾. The third of them: His saying ﴿innā fatahnā laka﴾ (Indeed, We have granted you a clear victory). Its aspect is that it was "narrated that the believers said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'Congratulations to you! Allah has forgiven you; what then is for us?' So this verse was revealed." It is as if He, exalted is He, said: Indeed We have opened for you a manifest victory so that He may forgive you, and We have opened (victory) for the believers so that He may admit them into gardens. As for if we say that this is understood not from speech but from the circumstance, we say: it is the command to fight, because from the mention of the opening and the victory it is known that the situation is one of fighting. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, commanded fighting so that He might admit the believers. Or we say: it is known from the circumstantial indicator that Allah chose the believers so that He might admit them into gardens.

Fourth issue: Here and in some other places He said "al-mu'minīna wa-al-mu'mināt" (the believing men and the believing women), and in some places He sufficed with mentioning "al-mu'minīn" (the believers), and the believing women are included among them, as in His saying: ﴿wa-bashshiri al-mu'minīn﴾ [al-Ahzab: 47] and His saying: ﴿qad aflaḥa al-mu'minūn﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 1]. What is the wisdom in this? We say: in the places where there is something that gives the impression of restricting the believers to the promised reward, while the believing women share with them, Allah mentions them explicitly. In the places where there is nothing that gives that impression, He suffices with their inclusion among the believers. So His saying ﴿wa-bashshiri al-mu'minīn﴾, although it is known from His saying ﴿wa-mā arsalnāka illā kāffatan li-l-nāsi bashīran wa-nadhīran﴾ [Saba': 28] that the generality does not suggest the exclusion of the believing women from the good tidings, yet here, since His saying ﴿li-yudkhila al-mu'minīn﴾ is connected to a preceding act, which is either the command to fight, or steadfastness in it, or the help of the believers, or the opening by their hands, as might be supposed, because the admission of the believers was for fighting, and a woman does not fight, so she would not enter the promised Paradise, He explicitly mentioned them. Likewise regarding the hypocrites and the polytheists: a hypocritical woman and a polytheistic woman did not fight, so they would not be punished, and He explicitly mentioned them. Likewise in His saying ﴿inna al-muslimīna wa-al-muslimāt wa-al-mu'minīna wa-al-mu'mināt﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35], because the context is the mention of women and their conditions, given His saying ﴿wa-lā tabarrajna﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], ﴿wa-aqimna﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], ﴿wa-ātīna﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33], ﴿wa-aṭṭa'na﴾ [al-Ahzab: 33]. And His saying ﴿wa-dhkurna mā yutlā fī buyūtikunna﴾ [al-Ahzab: 34]. So their mention there is fundamental. But since men have the same great reward as women, He mentioned them and mentioned the women with a singular expression, without subordination, because of what we have explained, that the original mention of them is in that place.

Fifth issue: Allah, exalted is He, said ﴿wa-yukaffira ʿanhum sayyi'ātihim﴾ (and remove from them their misdeeds) after mentioning the admission, although the removal of misdeeds comes before the admission? We say: the answer to this is from two aspects. The first: the conjunction "wa" (and) does not require sequence.

The second: the removal of misdeeds, forgiveness and other things are consequences of the accountable person being among the people of Paradise, so He put the admission first in mention, in the sense that he is among the people of Paradise.

The third: that the removal is by clothing in robes of honour, which are in Paradise, and a person in Paradise has removed from him the bodily blemishes of humanity such as impurities, and the spiritual ones such as anger and desire; this is the removal, and the angelic qualities are established in him, and these are the most noble kinds of robes.

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿wa-kāna dhālika ʿinda Allāh fawzan ʿaẓīman﴾ (and that is with Allah a great attainment), there are two aspects to it:

The first, which is well known: that the admission and the removal, in the sight of Allah, are a great attainment. One says: "This matter is, in my view, in this manner," meaning, in my belief.

The second, which is stranger than it and closer to reason: that "ʿinda Allāh" (with Allah) is taken as a description of that, as if He, exalted is He, says: that is with Allah, meaning, on condition that it is with Allah, the Exalted, and it is described as being with Allah a great attainment, to the extent that entering Paradise, if there were not in it nearness to Allah through being with Him, would not be an attainment.

[Page 73]

Then His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women, who assume about Allah an assumption of evil. Upon them is a circle of evil. Allah has become angry with them, and has cursed them, and has prepared for them Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ ﴿To Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth, and Allah is ever Mighty and Wise.﴾

Know that He mentioned the hypocrites before the polytheists in many places, for several reasons. The first: they were more harmful to the believers than the open disbelievers, because the believer guarded himself against the open polytheist, but he would mix with the hypocrite, thinking well of his faith, while the hypocrite would disclose his secrets. The Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to this when he said: "Your worst enemy is your self which is between your two sides." The hypocrite is in the form of Satan, for he does not come to a person saying, "I am your enemy," but comes to him saying, "I am your friend." The open disbeliever differs from Satan in one respect. Also, the hypocrite expected to escape through deception, whereas the disbeliever does not know for certain that, if the believer prevails, he will ransom himself. So Allah first informed about the hypocrite. As for His saying ﴿who assume about Allah an assumption of evil﴾, this assumption may have several meanings:

The first: it is the assumption that Allah mentioned in this surah with His saying ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families﴾ [al-Fath: 12].

The second: the assumption of the polytheists about Allah in associating partners with Him, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They are only names you have named them, you and your fathers﴾ [al-Najm: 23], up to His saying: ﴿They follow only assumption, and assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28].

The third: their assumption that Allah does not see and does not know, as He said: ﴿And you assumed that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾ [Fussilat: 22]. The first is more sound. Or we may say: what is meant is all their assumptions, so that it includes their assumption that Allah does not give life to the dead, and that the world's creation is vain, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 27]. What supports this meaning is the definite article (al-) in al-su' (the evil), which we will mention in His saying ﴿an assumption of evil﴾. On this there are several meanings:

The first: what was chosen by the verifying scholars among the men of letters, namely that al-su' (evil) has become an expression for corruption, and al-sidq (truth) an expression for righteousness. One says: "I passed by a man of evil (sū')," meaning corrupt, and "I was asked about a man of truth (sidq)," meaning righteous. So when the combined phrase "a man of evil" conveys the meaning of "corrupt," the word su' alone carries the meaning of corruption. This is what al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj agreed upon, and what al-Zamakhshari chose. The verification of this is that evil in meanings is like corruption in bodies. One says: "his temperament became evil (sāa mizājuh)," "his character became evil (sāa khuluquh)," and "his assumption became evil (sāa ẓannuh)," just as one says: "the meat spoiled (fasada al-laḥm)," and "the air spoiled (fasada al-hawā')." Indeed, everything that becomes evil has become corrupt, and everything that has become corrupt has become evil, except that one of the two is used much more for meanings and the other for physical bodies. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾ [al-Rum: 41], and He said: ﴿Evil is what they used to do﴾ [al-Tawbah: 9]. This is what appears to me from the verification of their statements.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Upon them is a circle of evil﴾, meaning a circle of corruption, and corruption has encompassed them in such a way that there is no escape for them from it.

* * *

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Allah has become angry with them﴾, as an addition in benefit. For whoever is afflicted may be tested by it, so he is struck in order to be rewarded, and he may be struck in the manner of punishment. So His saying ﴿Allah has become angry with them﴾ indicates that what has encompassed them is in the manner of punishment. His saying ﴿and has cursed them﴾ is an additional benefit, for the one with whom anger is incurred may be such that the angry one is content with reproach, insult, or beating, and his anger does not lead to distancing the one who incurred it from his presence or expelling him from his door. But it may be such that anger leads to expulsion and distancing, so He said ﴿and has cursed them﴾ because the anger is severe. Then, when He had explained their state in this world, He explained their end in the next, saying: ﴿And He has prepared for them Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ His saying ﴿evil is it﴾ indicates the feminine gender of the place, Hell. One says: "This abode, what a good place (ni'ma al-makān)." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ has already been explained, but some issues remain concerning it:

The first issue: What is the benefit of repeating it? We say: To Allah are the soldiers of mercy and the soldiers of punishment, or the soldiers of Allah are His sending down, which may be for mercy and may be for punishment. So He mentioned them first to explain mercy toward the believers, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. And second, to explain the sending down of punishment upon the disbelievers.

[Page 74]

The second issue: There He said: ﴿And Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [al-Nisa': 17], and here He says: ﴿And Allah is ever Mighty and Wise﴾, because His saying ﴿To Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ — we have shown that the purpose of mentioning them is to indicate the severity of punishment, so He mentioned might, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Is not Allah Mighty, Lord of Retribution?﴾ [al-Zumar: 37], and He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So We seized them with the seizure of One Mighty and Omnipotent﴾ [al-Qamar: 42], and He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿The Mighty, the Compeller﴾ [al-Hashr: 23].

The third issue: He mentioned the soldiers of the heavens and the earth before the entry of the believers into Paradise, and mentions them here after mentioning the punishment of the disbelievers and the preparation of Hell. We say: there is a fine order in this, because Allah, may He be exalted, sends down the soldiers of mercy, so He admits the believers into Paradise honored and exalted, then He clothes them in the robes of honor by His saying ﴿and will remove from them their misdeeds﴾, as we have explained. Then they will have nearness and closeness, by His saying ﴿And that is with Allah a great triumph﴾. Then His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And that He may punish the hypocrite men and the hypocrite women, and the polytheist men and the polytheist women, who assume about Allah an assumption of evil. Know that He mentioned the hypocrites before the polytheists in many places, for several reasons. The first: they were more harmful to the believers than the open disbelievers, because the believer guarded himself against the open polytheist, but he would mix with the hypocrite, thinking well of his faith, while the hypocrite would disclose his secrets. The Prophet (ﷺ) pointed to this when he said: "Your worst enemy is your self which is between your two sides." The hypocrite is in the form of Satan, for he does not come to a person saying, "I am your enemy," but comes to him saying, "I am your friend." The open disbeliever differs from Satan in one respect. Also, the hypocrite expected to escape through deception, whereas the disbeliever does not know for certain that, if the believer prevails, he will ransom himself. So Allah first informed about the hypocrite. As for His saying ﴿who assume about Allah an assumption of evil﴾, this assumption may have several meanings:

The first: it is the assumption that Allah mentioned in this surah with His saying ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families﴾ [al-Fath: 12].

The second: the assumption of the polytheists about Allah in associating partners with Him, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿They are only names you have named them, you and your fathers﴾ [al-Najm: 23], up to His saying: ﴿They follow only assumption, and assumption avails nothing against the truth﴾ [al-Najm: 28].

The third: their assumption that Allah does not see and does not know, as He said: ﴿And you assumed that Allah does not know much of what you do﴾ [Fussilat: 22]. The first is more sound. Or we may say: what is meant is all their assumptions, so that it includes their assumption that Allah does not give life to the dead, and that the world's creation is vain, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿That is the assumption of those who disbelieve﴾ [Sad: 27]. What supports this meaning is the definite article (al-) in al-su' (the evil), which we will mention in His saying ﴿an assumption of evil﴾. On this there are several meanings:

The first: what was chosen by the verifying scholars among the men of letters, namely that al-su' (evil) has become an expression for corruption, and al-sidq (truth) an expression for righteousness. One says: "I passed by a man of evil (sū')," meaning corrupt, and "I was asked about a man of truth (sidq)," meaning righteous. So when the combined phrase "a man of evil" conveys the meaning of "corrupt," the word su' alone carries the meaning of corruption. This is what al-Khalil and al-Zajjaj agreed upon, and what al-Zamakhshari chose. The verification of this is that evil in meanings is like corruption in bodies. One says: "his temperament became evil (sāa mizājuh)," "his character became evil (sāa khuluquh)," and "his assumption became evil (sāa ẓannuh)," just as one says: "the meat spoiled (fasada al-laḥm)," and "the air spoiled (fasada al-hawā')." Indeed, everything that becomes evil has become corrupt, and everything that has become corrupt has become evil, except that one of the two is used much more for meanings and the other for physical bodies. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Corruption has appeared on land and sea﴾ [al-Rum: 41], and He said: ﴿Evil is what they used to do﴾ [al-Tawbah: 9]. This is what appears to me from the verification of their statements.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Upon them is a circle of evil﴾, meaning a circle of corruption, and corruption has encompassed them in such a way that there is no escape for them from it.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Allah has become angry with them﴾, as an addition in benefit. For whoever is afflicted may be tested by it, so he is struck in order to be rewarded, and he may be struck in the manner of punishment. So His saying ﴿Allah has become angry with them﴾ indicates that what has encompassed them is in the manner of punishment. His saying ﴿and has cursed them﴾ is an additional benefit, for the one with whom anger is incurred may be such that the angry one is content with reproach, insult, or beating, and his anger does not lead to distancing the one who incurred it from his presence or expelling him from his door. But it may be such that anger leads to expulsion and distancing, so He said ﴿and has cursed them﴾ because the anger is severe. Then, when He had explained their state in this world, He explained their end in the next, saying: ﴿And He has prepared for them Hell, and evil is it as a destination.﴾ His saying ﴿evil is it﴾ indicates the feminine gender of the place, Hell. One says: "This abode, what a good place (ni'ma al-makān)." His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the soldiers of the heavens and the earth﴾ has already been explained, but some issues remain concerning it:

So He mentioned them first to explain mercy toward the believers, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And He is ever merciful to the believers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43]. And second, to explain the sending down of punishment upon the disbelievers.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner﴾ ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honour him, and glorify Him morning and evening﴾.

The exegetes said: "Witness" (shahidan) means a witness over your community concerning what they do, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. But the better view is that Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness﴾ [al-Fath: 8], and by this he bears witness that there is no god but Allah, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He, and so do the angels and those of knowledge﴾ [Al 'Imran: 18]. These are the prophets, peace be upon them, to whom Allah gave knowledge from Himself and taught what they did not know. For this reason Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾, meaning, bear witness. His saying "bringer of good news" (mubashshiran) is for whoever accepts his testimony, acts upon it and agrees with him in it; and "warner" (nadhiran) is for whoever rejects his testimony and opposes him in it.

Then He explained the purpose of sending him in the manner He mentioned, saying: ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honour him, and glorify Him﴾. This admits of two interpretations:

The first: the four matters mentioned are arranged upon the matters mentioned before. His saying ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾ is arranged upon His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾, because his being a messenger sent by Allah requires that the responsible person believe in Allah who sent him and in the one sent. His saying ﴿as a witness﴾ requires that one support Allah and strengthen His religion, because his being "a witness", as we have explained its meaning, is that he bears witness that there is no god but Him; so His religion is the truth and more deserving of being followed. His saying ﴿and a bringer of good news﴾ requires that one honour Allah, because magnifying Allah in his sight is in the likeness of Allah's magnifying him. His saying ﴿and a warner﴾ requires that one be purified from evil and indecency out of fear of His painful punishment and severe retribution. The basic principle of sending is arranged upon the basic principle of faith, and the attribute of the Messenger is arranged upon it, and the attribute of the believer follows from it.

The second: each of these attributes requires all four matters. His being a messenger requires that the responsible person believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honour him and glorify Him. Likewise His being a witness to the Oneness (of Allah) requires the matters mentioned. Likewise His being ﴿a bringer of good news and a warner﴾. It may be objected that the attachment of the lam (li-) to a verb requires a preceding verb to which it is attached, and it is not attached to the attribute; and His saying ﴿so that you may believe﴾ requires a verb, which is His saying ﴿Indeed, We have sent you﴾. So how are the matters arranged upon His being ﴿a witness and a bringer of good news﴾? We say: arrangement upon it is possible in meaning, not in wording, just as when one says: "I sent to you a scholar so that you may honour him," the wording indicates that the sending is the cause of honouring, while in meaning his being a scholar is the cause of honouring. For this reason, if he said: "I sent to you an ignorant man so that you may honour him," it would be fine. When we want to combine wording and meaning, we say: the sending which is the sending in the state of his being a witness, just as you say: the sending of the scholar is the cause of making him a cause, neither the mere sending nor the mere scholar.

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: In al-Ahzab He said: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner﴾ ﴿and as one calling to Allah by His permission and a illuminating lamp﴾ [al-Ahzab: 45–46]. Here He restricted Himself to three of the five. What is the wisdom in this? We answer: the answer to it is from two aspects. The first: that place was a place of mentioning him, because most of the surah concerns the Messenger ﷺ, his circumstances, and what preceded it of the pledge, the promise and the entry, so it was detailed there and not detailed here. The second: we say that the speech is mentioned here because His saying ﴿witness﴾ did not necessarily imply that he is a caller, since it is possible that he says to himself "I bear witness that there is no god but Allah" without calling people; so there He said "and a caller to that". Here, since his being a ﴿witness﴾ did not indicate his being a caller, He said ﴿so that you may believe in Allah and His Messenger, support him, honour him and glorify Him﴾, which is evidence of his being a lamp, because he brought what is obligatory of magnification and of abstaining from what is forbidden of evil and indecency, by purification, which is glorification.

Second issue: We have mentioned repeatedly that the choice of morning and evening may indicate constancy, and it may be an instruction contrary to what the polytheists used to do, for they used to gather for the worship of idols in the Ka'bah in the morning and evening, so they were commanded to glorify Him at times when they used to mention indecency and wrong.

Third issue: The pronominal suffixes mentioned in His saying ﴿support him, honour him and glorify him﴾ refer to Allah, exalted is He, or to the Messenger, peace be upon him? The more correct view is the first.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah. The hand of Allah is above their hands. So whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment, and whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward.﴾

When He had explained that he (ﷺ) was sent as a messenger, He mentioned that whoever pledges allegiance to him has pledged allegiance to Allah. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾ admits of several interpretations. The word "hand" in the two places is either used with one meaning or with two meanings. If we say it has one meaning, then there are two views:

The first: ﴿The hand of Allah﴾ means the blessing of Allah upon them, which is above their kindness to Allah, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Rather, Allah confers favour upon you that He guided you to faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 17]. The second: ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾, that is, His help for them is stronger and higher than their help for Him. It is said: "The hand is for so-and-so," meaning dominance, victory and subjugation.

But if we say that it has two meanings, then we say that with regard to Allah, exalted is He, it means protection, and with regard to those who pledge allegiance, it means the limb. The hand is a metaphor for protection, derived from the situation of two contracting parties when each of them extends his hand to the other in buying and selling, and between them there is a third, intermediary party who does not want the contract to be dissolved without completing the sale. So he places his hand over their hands and protects their hands until the contract is completed, and does not let one of them abandon the other's hand. Thus placing the hand above the hands became a cause of safeguarding the pledge. Therefore He, exalted is He, said: ﴿The hand of Allah is above their hands﴾, protecting them in the pledge just as that intermediary protects the hands of the contracting parties.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So whoever breaks his oath, breaks it only to his own detriment﴾: as for our view that the meaning of "hand" is blessing or dominance and power, it is because whoever breaks (the pledge) forfeits for himself the abundant kindness in exchange for a small deed, so he has lost, and his breaking is to his own detriment. As for our view that the meaning is protection, the statement refers back to His saying: ﴿Indeed, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah﴾, meaning: whoever pledges allegiance to you, O Prophet, if he breaks it, his breaking does not return to you, because the pledge is with Allah and not to Allah, since He is not harmed by anything, so His harm does not return except to Him.

He said: ﴿And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, He will give him a great reward.﴾ We have mentioned that greatness in bodies is not said unless there is combined in it great length, wide breadth and thick depth. Thus a mountain that is high but has no breadth to its width is said to be a lofty, elevated or towering mountain; but when breadth in its sides is added to it, it is said to be great. The reward is likewise, because the foods of Paradise are of the highest kinds, are in the utmost abundance, and extend forever without cessation. So there is present in it what suits being called great. And greatness with regard to Allah, exalted is He, is an indication of His perfection in His attributes, just as in bodies it is an indication of its perfection in its dimensions.

Then God Most High said: "The disbelieving Arabs who stayed behind will say to you, 'Our possessions and our families kept us busy, so ask forgiveness for us.' They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts. Say: 'Who can avail you anything against God, if He intends harm for you or intends benefit for you? Rather, God is ever Aware of what you do.'" (48:11)

When He had explained the state of the hypocrites, He mentioned those who stayed behind. A group of the Bedouin refrained from going out with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), because they thought that he would be defeated. They said: "The people of Mecca are fighting at the gate of Medina, so what will their condition be when they enter their lands and the enemy surrounds them?" Then they offered excuses. Their saying "Our possessions and our families kept us busy" contains two points that make the excuse clear.

The first is their saying "our possessions" rather than "the possessions kept us busy." This is because the mere accumulation of wealth is not a valid excuse, since it has no end. However, guarding what has been gathered from being scattered, and protecting what has been acquired from being lost, is a valid excuse. Thus they said "our possessions kept us busy," meaning what has become our property, not possessions in general.

The second is His saying "and our families." This is because if someone said to them, "Wealth should not reach a level where its preservation prevents you from following the Messenger (ﷺ)," they could reply: "Family likewise prevents us, since preoccupation with them and their protection diverts us from the most important matters." Then, despite offering this excuse, they humbled themselves and said "so ask forgiveness for us," meaning: although we present our excuse, we acknowledge our wrongdoing, so ask forgiveness for us and pardon us regarding the matter of not going out. God rejected them, saying: "They say with their tongues what is not in their hearts."

This may bear two meanings. The first is that the denial refers to their saying "so ask forgiveness for us." Its realization is that they showed that they believed they had done wrong by staying behind, to the point of asking forgiveness, while in fact they did not believe this; rather, they believed that by staying behind they were doing good. The second is that their saying "kept us busy" indicates that their refusal was only for this reason, whereas that was not what they believed; rather, they believed their refusal was due to the belief that the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers would be overcome and defeated, as He said afterward: "Rather, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families again" (48:12).

His saying "Who can avail you anything against God, if He intends harm for you or intends benefit for you" means: you guard yourselves against harm, abandon the command of God and His Messenger, and sit back seeking safety. But if God intends harm for you, your sitting will not avail you anything against God. Or it means: you guard yourselves against the harm of fighting and those who fight, and you believe that your families and your lands will protect you from the enemy. Suppose you protected yourselves from that; who then will repel from you the punishment of God in the Hereafter? Yet that is more deserving of guarding against.

We mentioned in the commentary on Surah Ya Sin, in His saying "If the Most Merciful intends harm for me" (36:23), that when the speech is addressed to a believer, the particle "bi" (with) is attached to the harm, as in "If God intends harm for me" (39:38) and "If God touches you with harm" (6:17). When the speech is addressed to a disbeliever, the particle "bi" is attached to the disbeliever, as He says here: "if He intends harm for you," and He says: "Who is it that can protect you from God if He intends evil for you?" (33:17). We have mentioned the excellent distinction there, and we will not repeat it, so that this may be an incentive to study the commentary on Surah Ya Sin, for it is "the string of unique pearls."

His saying "Rather, God is ever Aware of what you do" means: of what you do by way of displaying war while concealing other than it.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Nay, you thought that the Messenger and the believers would never return to their families, and that was made attractive in your hearts, and you harbored an evil assumption, and you were a people doomed to perish.﴾

He means: your staying behind was not for the reasons you mentioned. ﴿Nay, you thought that they would never return.﴾ Here "an" (أنْ) is the lightened form of the heavy "inna," meaning: you first assumed it, and then Satan made your assumption attractive to you until you became certain of it. This is because Satan may embellish a doubt and add to it a semblance of plausibility by which the heedless person becomes certain, even though the intelligent person would not doubt it.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you harbored an evil assumption (ẓann al-sawʼ)﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: this conjunction indicates a difference, so that His saying "and you harbored an evil assumption" is other than what is in His saying "Nay, you thought." In that case the second assumption may mean: "and you assumed that God would break His promise," or "you assumed that the Messenger was lying in what he said."

The second: His saying "and you harbored an evil assumption" refers to what preceded, namely the assumption that they would not return, and it is in the manner of someone's saying: "I know this matter, and I know such-and-such," meaning this matter and not something else. It is as if He said: "Nay, you thought the thought that they would never return." Your assumption that is corrupt. We have already explained the verification concerning "evil assumption."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you were a people doomed (būr)﴾ admits of two interpretations. The first: you became doomed and perishing by that assumption. The second: you were already doomed in origin, and you harbored that corrupt assumption.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And whoever does not believe in God and His Messenger, then We have prepared for the disbelievers a blaze (saʻīr).﴾

According to our statement, that "and you harbored an evil assumption" is a different assumption from what is in His saying "Nay, you thought," is evident, because we have explained that this was their assumption that God would break His promise, or their assumption that the Messenger was lying. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, conveys the greatness of both matters together, because from the greatness of His dominion comes that His reward and His gift are at the utmost greatness, and His punishment and His retribution are likewise at the utmost severity and pain.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those who were left behind will say, when you set out to take spoils, "Leave us, that we may follow you."﴾

Allah made clear their lying in this, since whenever the march was toward spoils that they expected, they would say of their own accord: ﴿Leave us, that we may follow you.﴾ So if their wealth and families had preoccupied them on the day you called them to the people of Makkah, then why do they not busy themselves with their wealth on the day of the spoils? The intended spoils are the spoils of the people of Khaybar and their conquest. The Muslims took spoils, and no one was with them except those who were with them in Madinah. In His saying ﴿Those who were left behind will say﴾ there is a promise to the pledgers who complied of spoil, and to the laggards who opposed of deprivation.

[p. 79]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They wish to change the words of Allah. Say: "You will never follow us; thus has Allah said before."﴾

It admits of several aspects:

The first: it is what Allah said, that the spoil of Khaybar is for those who witnessed al-Hudaybiyah and pledged with it, and no one else. This is the most famous view among the exegetes (mufassirun) and the most apparent, in view of His saying: ﴿Thus has Allah said before.﴾

The second: "They wish to change the words of Allah" refers to His saying: ﴿And Allah was angry with them.﴾ This is because if they had followed you, they would have been in the position of the pledgers of the Pleasure (ahl al-Ridwan) who were promised spoil, and so they would be among those with whom Allah was pleased, as He said: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree﴾ [al-Fath: 18]. Then they would not be among those with whom Allah was angry, and so the words of Allah would have to be changed.

The third: when the people lagged behind, Allah informed the Prophet ﷺ of their inner state and showed him their hypocrisy, and that He intended to punish them. He said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿Say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]. So they wished to change that statement by going out with him. It may be said: the verse you mention concerns the expedition to Tabuk, not this event. We say: there is found here, in His saying ﴿You will never follow us﴾ in the form of negation, instead of "Do not follow us" in the form of prohibition, a subtle meaning: the Prophet ﷺ based the negation on Allah's report about them, being confident and certain of its truth, so he affirmed it firmly and said ﴿You will never follow us﴾, meaning: even if I permitted you and even if you wished and chose, that would not be accomplished for you, because Allah had informed of it.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿They will say, "Rather, you envy us."﴾

As a reply to His saying: ﴿Thus has Allah said before.﴾ It is as though they said: "Allah did not say this before; rather, you envy us." Here "bal" (بَلْ, "rather") is used for idrab (retraction or turning away from a previous statement), and what is turned away from is omitted in both places. Here, it is with the implied meaning "Allah did not say [thus]". Likewise, if it is asked: on what basis was the envy in their belief? We say: it is as though they said: "We were right not to go out, since they returned from al-Hudaybiyah without gain while we rested. If we go out with them and there is spoil, they will say, 'They gained spoil with us and did not toil with us.'"

Then He, exalted is He, said, replying to them as they had replied: ﴿Rather, they did not understand except a little.﴾ That is: they did not grasp from your saying "do not go out" anything beyond the apparent prohibition, and they did not understand its ruling except a little, so they interpreted it according to what they wanted and gave the reason as envy.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say to the Bedouins who were left behind: "You will be called to a people of great might; you will fight them, or they will submit. If you obey, Allah will give you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before, He will punish you with a painful punishment."﴾

When the Prophet ﷺ said ﴿Say, you will never follow us﴾ and said ﴿Say, you will never go out with me ever﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83], the laggards were a large group from scattered tribes. There was a need to clarify the acceptance of their repentance, for they did not persist in that, and they were not among those who were stubborn in hypocrisy. Rather, among them were some whose condition was good and whose affairs were righteous. So He made a sign for the acceptance of their repentance: that they would be called to fight a people of great might, and they would obey. This is unlike the condition of Tha'labah, who refused to pay zakat and then brought it, and the Prophet ﷺ did not accept it from him, and his condition remained, and none of the Companions accepted it from him. Likewise, the condition of these people would have continued, had He, exalted is He, not explained that they would be called, so that if they obeyed, they would be given a good reward, and none of the Companions would leave them following him. The difference between the condition of Tha'labah and the condition of these people is in two respects:

The first: it may be said that Tha'labah's condition did not change in Allah's knowledge, so no sign was made for his repentance. The Bedouins changed, for after the Prophet ﷺ no one among the hypocrites remained in hypocrisy, according to the madhhab of Ahl al-Sunnah (the People of the Sunnah).

The second: the need to clarify the condition of the large group and the vast multitude was more pressing, because without the clarification the matter would have led to strife (fitnah) breaking out among the divisions of the Muslims.

In His saying ﴿You will be called to a people of great might﴾ there are several aspects:

The most famous and most apparent is that they are Banu Hanifah, when they followed Musaylimah and Abu Bakr fought them.

The second: they are Persia and the Romans, whom 'Umar fought.

The third: Hawazin and Thaqif, whom the Prophet ﷺ fought. The strongest of the aspects is that the calling was from the Prophet ﷺ, though what is more apparent is other than this. As for the proof of the strength of this aspect, it is that Ahl al-Sunnah agreed that the affair of the Arabs in the time of the Prophet ﷺ became manifest, and none remained except an open disbeliever or a believer who was pious and pure. The Prophet ﷺ refrained from praying over the dead of the hypocrites, and the believers abandoned associating with them, to the extent that 'Ubadah ibn Ka'b, despite being among the believers, was not spoken to by the believers for a period. What Allah mentioned is a sign of the manifestation of the condition of whoever was a hypocrite. If their condition became manifest by other than this, there is no sense in making this a sign. And if it became manifest by this manifestation, it was in the time of the Prophet ﷺ, because if the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, had refused to accept them for following him, then Abu Bakr and 'Umar would have refused as well, in view of His saying: ﴿And follow him﴾ [al-A'raf: 158] and His saying: ﴿Follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31]. It may be said that this is weak for two reasons:

The first: the Prophet ﷺ said ﴿You will never follow us﴾ and said ﴿You will never go out with me ever﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83], so how could they follow him despite the negation?

The second: His saying ﴿of great might﴾, and after that there was no fighting of a people of great might left for the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace; for fear had taken hold of the hearts of people, and no might or strength remained after him. The agreement of the majority indicates strength and manifestation.

We say: As for the answer to the first, it is in two respects:

The first: that statement is restricted, its meaning being: "You will never go out with me ever, while you are as you are." This restriction is necessary, because we agree that among them were those who embraced Islam and whose Islam was good, indeed most of them. It was not permissible for the Prophet ﷺ to say to them, "You are not Muslims," in view of His saying: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisa': 94]. Given their profession of Islam, it was not permissible to prevent them from jihad in the way of Allah, though it was obligatory upon them, and this was restricted. Their good condition became clear, for the Prophet ﷺ called them to jihad, some of them obeyed him and others refused, their affair became manifest, and it became known who persisted in disbelief from among those whose hearts were firm in faith.

The second: what is meant by His saying ﴿You will never follow us﴾ is in this fighting alone, while His saying ﴿You will never go out with me﴾ was about something other than this, namely the hypocrites who stayed behind in the expedition to Tabuk.

As for the agreement of the majority, we say: there is no contradiction between us and them. We say: the Prophet ﷺ called them first, and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, also called them after he knew that this action of the Prophet ﷺ was permissible. We only affirm that the Prophet ﷺ called them. If they say that Abu Bakr called them, there is no conflict between the two statements. If they say that the Prophet ﷺ did not call them, then the negation and the firm assertion of it are extremely far-fetched, since it may be that this did occur. How could it not, when the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, said, from the words of Allah: ﴿If you love Allah, then follow me﴾ [Al 'Imran: 31], and said: ﴿And follow me; this is a straight path﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 61]?
