On the day of his saying ﷺ ﴿You will never follow us﴾, most of the Arabs were in disbelief and hypocrisy, since it was before the conquest of Makkah and before the taking of many fortresses.

As for his saying that the Prophet ﷺ had no fighting left with a people of great might, we say: we do not concede that, because the Prophet ﷺ in the year of al-Hudaybiyah called them to war, for he set out in ihram with the sacrificial animals so that Quraysh would know that he did not seek fighting, and they refused. So he said: ﴿You will be called to war.﴾ There is no doubt that one whose opponent is armed and fighting is greater in might than one whose opponent is not so. He knew from the condition of Makkah that they did not honor a pilgrim or a visitor. So His saying ﴿of great might﴾ means: possessors of weapons of iron, in which there is great might. As for the one who said that the caller was Abu Bakr and 'Umar, he held to the verse as evidence for their caliphate, and its indication is clear.

[p. 81]

"Will you fight them, or will they submit?" The "aw" (أوْ, "or") indicates that one of the two will occur. It was also read as "aw yuslimu" (أوْ يُسْلِمُوا) in the accusative, with "an" (أنْ) implied, meaning "you will fight them until they submit". The verification in this is that "aw" (أوْ) is only used between two different things, and it indicates restriction. One says: "The number is even or odd"; for this reason it is not valid to say: "He is Zayd or 'Amr." For this reason one says: "The number is even, or five, or other than these," when this is known. When a speaker says, "I will certainly stick to you, or you will pay me my right," it is understood from it that time is confined to two parts: a part in which there is sticking to him, and a part in which the right is paid. There is no time between sticking to him and paying the right in which neither sticking nor payment occurs. So in his saying "I will certainly stick to you or you pay me," it is like what is reported in the saying of one who says: "I will certainly stick to you until you pay me," because the duration of sticking extends until payment. This weakens the view of the one who says: the caller was 'Umar, and the people were Persia and the Romans, because both groups accept the jizya (poll tax on protected non-Muslims), so fighting them does not extend until they embrace Islam, since they may pay the jizya.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you obey, Allah will give you a good reward; but if you turn away as you turned away before﴾ contains a benefit, because turning away with an excuse, as He said: ﴿There is no blame on the blind﴾ [al-Nur: 61], does not bring a painful punishment upon the one who turns away. So He said: ﴿But if you turn away as you turned away﴾, meaning: if your turning away is based on a corrupt assumption and a false belief, as it was when you said with your tongues, not with your hearts, ﴿Our wealth and families occupied us﴾, then Allah will punish you with a painful punishment.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind, nor upon the lame, nor upon the sick﴾. He explained who is permitted to remain behind and abandon jihad, and what makes abandoning jihad permissible, namely whatever prevents one from advancing and retreating (al-karr wa'l-farr). He clarified this by specifying three categories. The first is (the blind), for he cannot advance against the enemy or pursue, nor can he take precautions or flee. The lame is likewise, and so is the sick. In the same sense as the lame are the one missing a limb (al-aqta') and the paralysed (al-muqʻad), and these are more deserving of being excused. Whoever has a limp that does not prevent him from advancing and retreating is not excused. Likewise, a slight illness that does not prevent advancing and retreating, such as an enlarged spleen (al-tuhal) or a cough, since by it one becomes weak. Some joint pains do not constitute an excuse. There are in this matter several issues:

The first issue: these are excuses that pertain to the person of the fighter itself. There are also external excuses, such as poverty, which prevents its bearer from taking along what he needs, and being occupied with someone who, were it not for him, would be lost, such as a child or a sick person. Excuses are known from jurisprudence (fiqh), and we are investigating here what relates to exegesis (tafsir), in explaining several issues:

The first issue: the mention of the excuses that apply during travel; for the others are removable, unlike lameness and blindness.

The second issue: only the three categories were mentioned, because an excuse is either a defect in a limb or a defect in strength. A defect caused by a limb is either a defect in the limb through which one reaches the enemy and moves in the places of battle, or in the limb through which the benefit of acquiring knowledge and reaching is completed. The first is the leg, and the second is the eye, because through the leg movement occurs, and through the eye benefit is gained in pursuing and fleeing. As for the ear, the nose, the tongue and other limbs, they have no bearing on either of these two matters. There remains the hand, for one who has lost both hands can do nothing, and this is a clear excuse, yet it was not mentioned. We say: because the benefit of the leg, which is movement, is nullified by a defect in one of them, whereas the benefit of the hand, which is striking and seizing, is not nullified except by the loss of both hands together. One who has lost both hands is found only rarely. Perhaps among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) there was no one who had lost both hands, so it was not mentioned; or because the one who has lost a hand can still be benefited in jihad, for he can be looked after, and without him a fighter would be alone, so he may fight; and he is not excused from remaining behind, because the mujahidin benefit from him. This is unlike the blind. If it is said: just as the loss of one hand does not nullify the benefit of its grip, so too the one-eyed does not lose the benefit of his sight, and yet the blind was mentioned, while the paralysed and the one who has lost both hands were not mentioned? We say: because we have explained that one who has lost both hands is rarely found, and a calamity striking one hand does not affect both, whereas a calamity striking one eye affects both eyes, because the source of light is one and the two are linked, and existence distinguishes between them, for the blind are numerous, while one who has lost both hands is rare.

The third issue: He placed the defect of the instrument before the defect of strength, because a defect of strength may cease or arise, whereas a defect of the instrument, once it arises, does not cease, for the blind does not return to sight. Thus the excuse in the place of the instrument is more complete.

The fourth issue: He placed the blind before the lame, because the blind man's excuse persists even if he attends the battle, whereas the lame, if he attends riding or by another route, can fight by shooting and other means.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, and whoever turns away, He will punish him with a painful punishment﴾. ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down tranquillity upon them and rewarded them with a near victory﴾. ﴿And abundant spoils which they will take. And Allah is ever Exalted in Might, Wise﴾.

Know that the obedience to each of the two is obedience to the other, so they were joined together to clarify the obedience to Allah. For if He had said, "Whoever obeys Allah," some people might have said, "We do not see Allah nor hear His speech, so from where do we know His command that we may obey Him?" Therefore He said: His obedience is in the obedience to His Messenger, and His speech is heard from His Messenger.

* * *

Then, when He had explained the condition of those who stayed behind after His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are actually pledging allegiance to Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 10], He returned to explaining their condition, and said: ﴿Allah was certainly pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree, and He knew what was in their hearts﴾, of sincerity, just as He knew what was in the hearts of the hypocrites of sickness ﴿so He sent down tranquillity upon them﴾ until they pledged allegiance upon death. Likewise, a slight illness that does not prevent advancing and retreating, such as an enlarged spleen (al-tuhal) or a cough, since by it one becomes weak. Some joint pains do not constitute an excuse. There are in this matter several issues:

The first issue: these are excuses that pertain to the person of the fighter itself. There are also external excuses, such as poverty, which prevents its bearer from taking along what he needs, and being occupied with someone who, were it not for him, would be lost, such as a child or a sick person. Excuses are known from jurisprudence (fiqh), and we are investigating here what relates to exegesis (tafsir), in explaining several issues:

The first issue: the mention of the excuses that apply during travel; for the others are removable, unlike lameness and blindness.

The second issue: only the three categories were mentioned, because an excuse is either a defect in a limb or a defect in strength. A defect caused by a limb is either a defect in the limb through which one reaches the enemy and moves in the places of battle, or in the limb through which the benefit of acquiring knowledge and reaching is completed. The first is the leg, and the second is the eye, because through the leg movement occurs, and through the eye benefit is gained in pursuing and fleeing. As for the ear, the nose, the tongue and other limbs, they have no bearing on either of these two matters. There remains the hand, for one who has lost both hands can do nothing, and this is a clear excuse, yet it was not mentioned. We say: because the benefit of the leg, which is movement, is nullified by a defect in one of them, whereas the benefit of the hand, which is striking and seizing, is not nullified except by the loss of both hands together. One who has lost both hands is found only rarely. Perhaps among the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) there was no one who had lost both hands, so it was not mentioned; or because the one who has lost a hand can still be benefited in jihad, for he can be looked after, and without him a fighter would be alone, so he may fight; and he is not excused from remaining behind, because the mujahidin benefit from him. This is unlike the blind. If it is said: just as the loss of one hand does not nullify the benefit of its grip, so too the one-eyed does not lose the benefit of his sight, and yet the blind was mentioned, while the paralysed and the one who has lost both hands were not mentioned? We say: because we have explained that one who has lost both hands is rarely found, and a calamity striking one hand does not affect both, whereas a calamity striking one eye affects both eyes, because the source of light is one and the two are linked, and existence distinguishes between them, for the blind are numerous, while one who has lost both hands is rare.

The third issue: He placed the defect of the instrument before the defect of strength, because a defect of strength may cease or arise, whereas a defect of the instrument, once it arises, does not cease, for the blind does not return to sight. Thus the excuse in the place of the instrument is more complete.

The fourth issue: He placed the blind before the lame, because the blind man's excuse persists even if he attends the battle, whereas the lame, if he attends riding or by another route, can fight by shooting and other means.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God has promised you many spoils that you will take, and He has hastened this for you, and restrained the hands of the people from you, and that it may be a sign for the believers, and that He may guide you to a straight path﴾.

Concerning the promised spoils there are several opinions, the soundest of which is that He promised them many spoils without specifying them, and all that they gained was among them, and God knew of them. This is like a generous king saying to one who serves him: "There will be a reward from me for what you have done, God willing," without intending any particular thing; then everything he brings and gives him falls under that promise, except that the king does not know the details of what reaches him at the time of the promise, whereas God knows them.

As for His saying, ﴿and He restrained the hands of the people from you﴾, it is for the completion of the favor, as if He said: "I provided you with a spoil that comes cool, without touching the heat of battle; and had you toiled in it, you would have said: 'This is the reward of our toil.'" Likewise His saying, ﴿so He hastened this for you﴾, [means] "so that it may benefit you," ﴿and that it may be a sign for the believers﴾. Or we may say its meaning is: that it may benefit you outwardly and benefit you inwardly, since your certainty increases when you see the truthfulness of the Messenger in his report of the unseen, so your reports become beautiful and your belief is perfected. As for His saying, ﴿and that He may guide you to a straight path﴾, this is trust in Him, entrusting oneself to Him, and taking pride in Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women, whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge﴾.

The description of the men and the women: that is, were it not for men and women who are believers but not known. His saying, ﴿that you might trample them﴾ (an tatawhum), is a substitute of inclusion, as if he said: men whose trampling was not known, so that there would befall you from them a disgrace—a reproach or a sin. That is because you might perhaps kill them, and then expiation would be obligatory upon you, which is a sign of sin; or the disbelievers would reproach you for having done to their brethren what they had done to their enemies. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿without knowledge﴾, al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying ﴿that you might trample them﴾, meaning that you might trample them without knowledge; and it is permissible that it be a substitute for the pronoun in His saying ﴿you did not know them﴾. Someone might object that this would be a repetition, because on our view, where it is a substitute for the pronoun, the sense would be: "you did not know that you might trample them without knowledge," so that "without knowledge" would be repeated by His saying "you did not know them." Rather, it is better to say that "without knowledge" is in its proper place, its sense being: "you did not know that you might trample them, whereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge"—who would disgrace you and reproach you. That is, if you trampled them unknowingly, the disgrace of the disbelievers would befall you (without knowledge), i.e., in ignorance, they not knowing that you are excused in it. Or we may say: its sense is "you did not know that you might trample them, whereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge," i.e., you would kill them without knowledge, or harm them without knowledge; so the trampling is the cause of the killing, and the trampling is not known to you, and the killing which is the cause of the disgrace is the trampling which occurs without knowledge. Or we may say: the disgrace is of two kinds:

The first: that which results from deliberate killing by one who does not know the state of the place.

The second: that which results from killing by mistake, which is not the absence of knowledge; so He said: there would befall you from them a disgrace that is not known, not one that arises from knowledge. (The answer of) "were it not" (lawla) is omitted; its sense is: "were it not for that, He would not have restrained your hands from them." This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and it is good. It may also be said that its answer is what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, meaning: they had deserved not to be left alone; and were it not for believing men, what they deserved would have befallen them, just as one says: "He is a thief, and were it not for so-and-so, I would have cut off his hand." This is because lawla is used only to express the prevention of one thing by the existence of another, and the prevention of a thing occurs only when its requisite has existed and something else has prevented it. So Allah first mentioned the complete and fully sufficient requisite, namely disbelief, barring, and hindering, and then mentioned the cause for which its requisite was prevented, namely the existence of believing men.

We say: the answer to this is in two respects:

The second: we have shown that the answer to lawla is what is indicated by His saying ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾; so it is as if He said: "They are the ones who disbelieved and deserved to be hastened in their destruction; and were it not for men, He would have hastened them; but He restrained your hands, that He might admit."

Another: it is said: He did what He did in order that He might admit; for there are acts of kindness, guidance and other things, and His saying ﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾ means: that among them those whom Allah knew would believe in that year might believe, or that they might leave Makkah and emigrate, and so He would admit them into His mercy. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Had they been separated﴾, means: had they been distinguished. The pronoun may be taken to refer to the believing men and the believing women. If it is said: how is this correct, when you have said that the answer to lawla is omitted, namely His saying "had He not restrained" or "He would have hastened"; and if ﴿had they been separated﴾ refers to the men, then "We would have punished" would be the answer to lawla? We say: al-Zamakhshari also said this, stating: ﴿had they been separated﴾ includes the mention of lawla, so it is possible that "We would have punished" is the answer to lawla. It may also be said that the pronoun refers to "whom He wills," as if He said: "that He may admit whom He wills into His mercy, had they separated themselves, distinguished themselves, and believed, We would have punished those whom Allah had decreed would not believe." And there are discussions here:

The first discussion: on the supposition we posit, the speech conveys that the painful punishment was averted from them, either because of the absence of separation or because of the existence of the believing men, and the existence of the believing men was known to be assumed; but the painful punishment is not averted from the disbeliever. We say: what is meant is a hastened punishment at your hands, which begins with the species, since they were not joined or turned toward them so that they would prevail and gain power; it would be painful.

The second discussion: what is the wisdom in mentioning the believing men and the believing women, when the feminine is included within the masculine in a group? We say: the answer to this is in two respects:

One of them: what has preceded, namely that the context is one in which one might wrongly think the ruling is restricted to men; for His saying ﴿you might trample them, whereby there would befall you﴾ means "you might destroy them," and the intent is: do not fight and do not kill. So the preventing factor was the existence of believing men, and He then said "and believing women also," because the ruin of their homes and the orphaning of their children on account of their men is a grievous burden.

The second: that in a place of compassion, the situations are enumerated to soften the heart. One says to someone who is punishing a person: do not punish him, and have mercy on his humiliation, his poverty, and his weakness; and one says: his children, his little ones, and his family are weak and helpless. Likewise here He said: ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women﴾, to soften the hearts of the believing women and to secure their acceptance of what took place of restraint after victory.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And it is He who restrained their hands from you and your hands from them in the heart of Makkah, after He had given you victory over them.﴾

This is an explanation of what preceded in His saying: ﴿And if those who disbelieved had fought you, they would have turned their backs.﴾ That is, it is by the decree of Allah, for He restrained their hands from you by their fleeing, and your hands from them by your turning back from them and leaving them alone. His saying, ﴿in the heart of Makkah﴾, is a reference to a matter that was there which required that restraint not occur, yet the restraining of hands nevertheless took place. That matter is the entry of the Muslims into the heart of Makkah, for that requires that the one being restrained be patient in fighting, because the enemy has entered his home seeking vengeance for them. This necessitates the utmost effort of the one who is weak in defending the sanctuary, and requires that the Muslims exert themselves greatly in jihad, for if they fell short they would be broken and taken captive, since their place of safety is far away. Therefore His saying, ﴿in the heart of Makkah﴾, is a reference to the remoteness of the restraint, and yet it occurred by the will of Allah, exalted is He. His saying, ﴿after He had given you victory over them﴾, is suitable for two matters. The first: that it is a favour upon the believers that the victory was theirs, even though the apparent circumstances would have called for the victory to be theirs (the enemy's), because the land belonged to them and because of their great numbers. The second: that He mentioned two matters preventing the first two matters, even though Allah had realised both of them with the hypocrites. As for the restraint of the hands of the disbelievers, it was remote, because they were in their own lands defending their families and children; and to this He alluded with His saying, ﴿in the heart of Makkah﴾. As for the restraint of the hands of the Muslims, it is because it came after they had gained victory over them, and whenever a person gains victory over his enemy, whom, had the enemy gained victory over him, he would have uprooted, it is remote for him to hold back from him; yet Allah restrained both hands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is ever Seeing of what you do.﴾

That is: Allah saw in it a benefit, even though you did not see that. He clarified this with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram and the sacrifice detained from reaching its place of sacrifice﴾ [al-Fath: 25], up to His saying: ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women﴾ [al-Fath: 25]. That is: the restraint was a safeguarding of the Muslims who were in Makkah, so that they might leave from it and enter it in a manner in which there would be no harm to the believing men and believing women within it. The exegetes differed concerning that restraint. Some of them said: what is meant is that which occurred in the year of the Conquest. Others said: that which occurred in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, for the Muslims routed the army of the disbelievers until they drove them into their houses. It was also said: the fighting was with stones.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram and the sacrifice detained from reaching its place of sacrifice.﴾

This is an indication that the restraint was not due to any merit in them, for they disbelieved, barred, and were besieged, and all of that necessitates fighting them. Thus it is not to be supposed that the two parties had agreed, that no disagreement remained between them, and that they had made peace, with no dispute remaining between them. Rather the disagreement persists and the dispute continues, because they are ﴿the ones who disbelieved and barred you﴾ and prevented you, so they increased in disbelief and enmity. And that [restraint] was only for the believing men and believing women. His saying, ﴿and the sacrifice﴾ (wal-hadya), is in the accusative on account of its coordination with the "kam" in ﴿barred you﴾; it is permissible to put it in the genitive by coordinating it with al-Masjid (i.e., "and from the sacrifice"). ﴿Detained﴾ (ma'kufan) is a circumstantial accusative, and ﴿that it reach﴾ (an yablugha) is to be read as "from reaching"; it may also be said that ﴿that it reach its place of sacrifice﴾ is in the nominative, its implied sense being "its reaching its place of sacrifice being detained", as one says: "I saw Zayd, his might being severe." "Detained" (ma'kufan) means prevented, and on this reading there is no need to supply "from" (ʿan).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women, whom you did not know, that you might trample them and thereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge﴾.

The description of the men and the women: that is, were it not for men and women who are believers but not known. His saying, ﴿that you might trample them﴾ (an tatawhum), is a substitute of inclusion, as if he said: men whose trampling was not known, so that there would befall you from them a disgrace—a reproach or a sin. That is because you might perhaps kill them, and then expiation would be obligatory upon you, which is a sign of sin; or the disbelievers would reproach you for having done to their brethren what they had done to their enemies. As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿without knowledge﴾, al-Zamakhshari said: it is connected to His saying ﴿that you might trample them﴾, meaning that you might trample them without knowledge; and it is permissible that it be a substitute for the pronoun in His saying ﴿you did not know them﴾. Someone might object that this would be a repetition, because on our view, where it is a substitute for the pronoun, the sense would be: "you did not know that you might trample them without knowledge," so that "without knowledge" would be repeated by His saying "you did not know them." Rather, it is better to say that "without knowledge" is in its proper place, its sense being: "you did not know that you might trample them, whereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge"—who would disgrace you and reproach you. That is, if you trampled them unknowingly, the disgrace of the disbelievers would befall you (without knowledge), i.e., in ignorance, they not knowing that you are excused in it. Or we may say: its sense is "you did not know that you might trample them, whereby there would befall you from them a disgrace without knowledge," i.e., you would kill them without knowledge, or harm them without knowledge; so the trampling is the cause of the killing, and the trampling is not known to you, and the killing which is the cause of the disgrace is the trampling which occurs without knowledge. Or we may say: the disgrace is of two kinds:

The first: that which results from deliberate killing by one who does not know the state of the place.

The second: that which results from killing by mistake, which is not the absence of knowledge; so He said: there would befall you from them a disgrace that is not known, not one that arises from knowledge. (The answer of) "were it not" (lawla) is omitted; its sense is: "were it not for that, He would not have restrained your hands from them." This is what al-Zamakhshari said, and it is good. It may also be said that its answer is what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, meaning: they had deserved not to be left alone; and were it not for believing men, what they deserved would have befallen them, just as one says: "He is a thief, and were it not for so-and-so, I would have cut off his hand." This is because lawla is used only to express the prevention of one thing by the existence of another, and the prevention of a thing occurs only when its requisite has existed and something else has prevented it. So Allah first mentioned the complete and fully sufficient requisite, namely disbelief, barring, and hindering, and then mentioned the cause for which its requisite was prevented, namely the existence of believing men.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills. Had they been separated, We would have punished those who disbelieved among them with a painful punishment﴾. Concerning this there are discussions:

The first: concerning the verb that requires the lam by which the admission occurs; and there are several views:

One of them: it is said that it is His saying ﴿restrained their hands from you﴾, [the purpose being] ﴿that He may admit﴾. One may not object that you have mentioned the preventing factor as the existence of believing men, so it would be as if He said: "He restrained your hands lest you trample them," so how can it be for something else? We say: the answer to this is in two respects:

One of them: we say: He restrained your hands lest you trample them, in order that you might enter, just as one says: "I fed him that he might be satisfied, that God might forgive me," i.e., the feeding was for the satisfied one, and it was so that God might forgive me.

The second: we have shown that the answer to lawla is what is indicated by His saying ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved﴾; so it is as if He said: "They are the ones who disbelieved and deserved to be hastened in their destruction; and were it not for men, He would have hastened them; but He restrained your hands, that He might admit."

Another: it is said: He did what He did in order that He might admit; for there are acts of kindness, guidance and other things, and His saying ﴿That Allah may admit into His mercy whom He wills﴾ means: that among them those whom Allah knew would believe in that year might believe, or that they might leave Makkah and emigrate, and so He would admit them into His mercy. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Had they been separated﴾, means: had they been distinguished. The pronoun may be taken to refer to the believing men and the believing women. If it is said: how is this correct, when you have said that the answer to lawla is omitted, namely His saying "had He not restrained" or "He would have hastened"; and if ﴿had they been separated﴾ refers to the men, then "We would have punished" would be the answer to lawla? We say: al-Zamakhshari also said this, stating: ﴿had they been separated﴾ includes the mention of lawla, so it is possible that "We would have punished" is the answer to lawla. It may also be said that the pronoun refers to "whom He wills," as if He said: "that He may admit whom He wills into His mercy, had they separated themselves, distinguished themselves, and believed, We would have punished those whom Allah had decreed would not believe." And there are discussions here:

The first discussion: on the supposition we posit, the speech conveys that the painful punishment was averted from them, either because of the absence of separation or because of the existence of the believing men, and the existence of the believing men was known to be assumed; but the painful punishment is not averted from the disbeliever. We say: what is meant is a hastened punishment at your hands, which begins with the species, since they were not joined or turned toward them so that they would prevail and gain power; it would be painful.

The second discussion: what is the wisdom in mentioning the believing men and the believing women, when the feminine is included within the masculine in a group? We say: the answer to this is in two respects:

One of them: what has preceded, namely that the context is one in which one might wrongly think the ruling is restricted to men; for His saying ﴿you might trample them, whereby there would befall you﴾ means "you might destroy them," and the intent is: do not fight and do not kill. So the preventing factor was the existence of believing men, and He then said "and believing women also," because the ruin of their homes and the orphaning of their children on account of their men is a grievous burden.

The second: that in a place of compassion, the situations are enumerated to soften the heart. One says to someone who is punishing a person: do not punish him, and have mercy on his humiliation, his poverty, and his weakness; and one says: his children, his little ones, and his family are weak and helpless. Likewise here He said: ﴿And were it not for believing men and believing women﴾, to soften the hearts of the believing women and to secure their acceptance of what took place of restraint after victory.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿When those who disbelieved put into their hearts zealotry, the zealotry of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance), then God sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and made them adhere to the word of piety, and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it, and God is ever Knowing of all things﴾.

"إذْ" (idh, "when") may be an adverb of time (ẓarf), in which case it requires a verb in which it occurs and which governs it. It may also be a direct object (maf'ūl bihi). If we say it is an adverb of time, then the verb occurring in it may be said to be expressed, or it may be said to be implied and not expressed. If we say it is expressed, there are two views:

The first is God's words: ﴿and they barred you﴾, meaning: they barred you at the time when they put zealotry into their hearts.

The second is God's words: ﴿We would have punished those of them who disbelieved﴾, meaning: We would have punished them at the time when they put zealotry into their hearts. The second is closer, because of its proximity in wording and its strong relevance in meaning, since when they put zealotry into their hearts they do not return to submission and compliance, and the believers, when God sent down tranquility upon them, do not abandon striving in jihad, and God is with the believers, so they punish the disbelievers with a painful punishment, or [they punish] the non-believers.

If we say that this is an implied, unexpressed element, then there are two views:

The first: God protected the believers from trampling upon them, and they are those who disbelieved, those into whose hearts He put zealotry.

The second: God has been gracious to you when those who disbelieved put zealotry into their hearts. On this view, God's words ﴿then God sent down His tranquility﴾ are an explanation of that graciousness.

If we say that it is a direct object, then the governing element is implied, its estimate being: "Remember," meaning: remember that time, just as you say: "Do you remember when Zayd stood?" meaning: "Do you remember the time of his standing?" just as you say: "Do you remember Zayd?" On this view, the time-adverb that is annexed to it governs it. In this there are subtle points, both semantic and verbal.

The first: God, exalted is He, made manifest the utmost difference between the disbeliever and the believer, and He indicated three things:

One: He attributed to the disbelievers what they did by their own making, saying: ﴿when those who disbelieved made﴾, and He attributed to the believers what was made by God's making, saying: ﴿then God sent down﴾; and the difference between the two agents is not hidden.

Two: He made zealotry for the disbelievers and tranquility for the believers, and between the two objects there is a difference, as we will mention.

Three: He annexed zealotry to the Jahiliyyah, and annexed tranquility to Himself, when He said: ﴿zealotry of the Jahiliyyah﴾ and said: ﴿His tranquility﴾; and between the two annexations there is what cannot be mentioned.

The second: He increased the believers in goodness after the occurrence of a contrast of one thing with another: their act with God's act, zealotry with tranquility, and annexation to the Jahiliyyah with annexation to God, exalted is He: ﴿and made them adhere to the word of piety﴾, and we will mention its meaning.

As for the verbal subtleties, there are three:

The first: He said regarding the disbeliever: "made" (ja'ala), and He said regarding the believer: "sent down" (anzala), and He did not say "created" (khalaqa), nor "made His tranquility" (ja'ala sakīnatahu), indicating that zealotry was made in the present state, in an accident that does not endure, whereas tranquility was like something preserved in the treasury of mercy, prepared for His servants, so He sent it down.

The second: He said "zealotry" and then annexed it with His words: ﴿zealotry of the Jahiliyyah﴾, because zealotry in itself is a blameworthy attribute, and by being annexed to the Jahiliyyah it becomes even uglier, and zealotry has a degree of ugliness in which the ugliness of all ugly things is not considered, like what is annexed to the Jahiliyyah. As for tranquility, in itself, although it is good, the annexation to God in it contains a goodness such that no consideration of goodness remains alongside it, so He said: ﴿His tranquility﴾, being content with the goodness of the annexation.

The third: His words: "fa-anzala" (then He sent down) with the fā' rather than the wāw, indicating that this is like a reciprocal exchange. You say: "He honored me, so I honored him," for reciprocity and exchange. Had you said: "He honored me and I honored him," it would not indicate that. On this basis there is a subtlety: when the anger of one of two enemies intensifies, the other enemy is either weak or strong. If he is weak, he is routed and subdued; if he is strong, his anger produces anger in him, and this is the cause of the rise of strife and fighting. So [God] said, regarding the very movement at the time of their movement: "We did not advance, and we did not retreat."

God's words: "fa-anzala Allāh" (so God sent down) with the fā' indicate that the sending down is connected to the fā', which points to its being arranged upon something. We say that there are two views:

The first: what we have mentioned, that "idh" is an adverb of time, as if He said: "God has been gracious when those who disbelieved made [zealotry]," and His words "then He sent down" are an explanation of that graciousness, just as one says: "He honored me, so he gave me," explaining the honor.

The second: that the fā' is for indicating that the connection of the sending down of tranquility to their putting zealotry into their hearts is in the sense of reciprocity. You say: "He honored me, so I praised him." It is also permissible that they are two acts occurring without reciprocity, just as you say: "Zayd came to me and 'Amr went out." Here it is like that, because when they put zealotry into their hearts, the Muslims, according to the normal course of things, if you looked at them, it would follow that one of two things would come from them: either advance, or retreat. For when the anger of one of two enemies intensifies, the other enemy, if he is equal to him in strength, also becomes angry, and this stirs up strife; and if he is weaker than him, he retreats or submits to him. So God, exalted is He, sent down in return for the zealotry of the disbelievers upon the believers His tranquility, so that they did not become angry and did not retreat, but rather they were patient. This is remote in the normal course of things, so it is from God's bounty, exalted is He.

God's words: ﴿upon His Messenger and upon the believers﴾: He is the one who agreed to the peace with the disbelievers, and the believers had in themselves [the intention] not to return except with one of three [outcomes]: by sacrificing at the place of sacrifice, and they refused that [the words] "Muhammad, Messenger of God" and "In the name of God" not be written. So when the Messenger of God ﷺ became calm, the believers became calm.

God's words: ﴿and made them adhere to the word of piety﴾ have several interpretations. The most evident of them is that it is the saying: "There is no god but God," for by it protection from shirk is achieved. It was said: it is "In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful" and "Muhammad is the Messenger of God," for the disbelievers refused that and the believers adhered to it. It was said: it is the fulfilment of the covenant, and other [interpretations]. We will clarify which of these is preponderant by evidence, so we say: ﴿and made them adhere﴾ may refer to the Prophet ﷺ and the believers all together, meaning: He made the Prophet and the believers adhere to the word of piety. It may also refer to the believers alone. If we say that it refers to both of them together, then it is the command to piety, for God, exalted is He, said to the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿O Prophet, fear God and do not obey the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], and He said to the believers: ﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102]. And the command to fear God to the extent that His fear distracts one from turning to anything other than God, just as He said regarding the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿fear God and do not obey the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1], and God said: ﴿and you fear people, while God has more right that you fear Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. Then He explained to him the condition of those who believed him, with His words: ﴿who convey the messages of God and fear Him and fear none but God﴾ [al-Ahzab: 39]. As for regarding the believers, He said: ﴿O you who believe, fear God as He should be feared﴾ [Al 'Imran: 102], and He said: ﴿so do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 3]. And if we say that it refers to the believers, then it is His words: ﴿And whatever the Messenger gives you, take it, and whatever he forbids you, desist﴾ [al-Hashr: 7]. Do you not see [how it connects] to His words: "and fear God," which is His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not put yourselves forward before God and His Messenger﴾ [al-Hujurat: 1]? And in His words: ﴿and made them adhere to the word of piety﴾, on this [view] there is a subtle meaning, which is that when He, exalted is He, says "fear [God]," the command is a given; then among people there are those who accept it by God's guidance and adhere to it, and among them are those who do not adhere to it. Whoever adheres to it has adhered to it by God's making it binding upon him. So it is as if He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and made them adhere to the word of piety﴾. In this meaning there is preponderance, insofar as piety, although it is complete, is nearer to the "word." On this basis, His words: ﴿and they were more deserving of it and worthy of it﴾ mean that they were, in God's sight, the most honored of people, so they were made to adhere to His piety. This is because God's words: ﴿Indeed the most honored of you in God's sight is the most pious of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13] may bear two interpretations:

One: that its meaning is that whoever has more piety, God honors him more.

The second: that its meaning is that whoever will be more honored in God's sight and nearer to Him is more pious, as in the saying: "and the sincere are in great peril" [a saying], and God's words: ﴿those who are, out of fear of their Lord, apprehensive﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 57]. On the second interpretation, the meaning of His words: ﴿and they were more deserving of it﴾ is that they were more knowing of God, according to His words: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear God﴾ [Fatir: 28]. And His words: ﴿and worthy of it﴾ may bear two interpretations:

One: that from the meaning of "more deserving" it is understood that it establishes a preference over the disbelievers, even if it does not establish worthiness, just as if a king chose two men for a task, each of whom is unfit for it, but one of them is further from eligibility; then he said of the nearer one to eligibility: "If there must be one, then this one is more deserving," just as one says: "Imprisonment is easier than killing," though there is no ease there at all. So He said: ﴿and worthy of it﴾ to repel that.

The second, which is stronger, is to say: God's words: ﴿and worthy of it﴾ have several meanings, which we will clarify after we clarify the meaning of "more deserving." We say it may bear two interpretations:

One: that "more deserving" (aḥaqq) is in the sense of "true" (ḥaqq), not as a comparative, as in His words: ﴿better in station﴾ and ﴿finer in assembly﴾ [Maryam: 73], since there is no good in anything other than it.

The second: that it is comparative, and this may bear two interpretations:

One: that it is in relation to others, i.e., the believers are more deserving than the disbelievers.

The second: that it is in relation to the word of piety compared with another word that is not piety. You say: "Zayd is more deserving of honor than of humiliation," just as when a person asks about Zayd whether he is more knowledgeable in medicine or in jurisprudence, and you say: "He is more knowledgeable in jurisprudence," meaning: more than in medicine.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled His Messenger's vision with truth: you will surely enter the Sacred Mosque, if Allah wills, in security, with your heads shaved and your hair cut short, without fear.﴾ [He knew what you did not know, and He granted, besides that, a near victory.]

This is an explanation of the corruption of what the hypocrites said after Allah sent down tranquility (al-sakinah) upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and their stopping at what they had been commanded, namely not to advance into fighting. Their words were: "We did not enter the Sacred Mosque, nor did we shave our heads, nor did we cut our hair short." This was because the Prophet ﷺ had seen in his dream that the believers would enter Makkah and complete the Hajj, but he had not specified a time for it. So he related his dream to the believers, and they were certain that the matter was as the Prophet ﷺ had seen in his dream. They assumed that the entry would happen in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, while Allah knew that it would not happen except in the year of the Conquest (al-Fath). When they made the treaty and returned, the hypocrites said, mocking: "We did not enter, nor did we shave." Then the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, Allah fulfilled His Messenger's vision with truth.﴾

The transitive use of ṣadaqa (to make true, to fulfil) with two objects may be taken as direct, and it is of those verbs that take two objects, like the word ja'ala (to make) and khalaqa (to create). It may also be said that it is transitive to "the vision" through a preposition, its implied sense being: "Allah made His Messenger truthful in the vision." On the first reading, its meaning is: He made it an event that lies between the truth of His promise, when the promised thing occurred and was brought about. On the second reading, its meaning is: what Allah showed him was not false in it. On this basis, it may be that he saw in his dream that Allah, the Most High, was saying: "You will surely enter the Sacred Mosque." Then the phrase "fulfilled" (ṣadaqa) is apparent, because the use of ṣidq (truth) in speech is apparent. It may also be that peace and blessings be upon him saw that he was entering the Mosque, and then the phrase ﴿Allah fulfilled﴾ means that he brought about what makes the dream real. This indicates that it is true, as one says: "The age of his camel's tooth fulfilled me," and in the case where he realised the matter which he showed himself, it is taken from camels when it is said to them: hidda' (be calm), and they were calmed, so that it was realised that they were young camels, for hidda' is a word with which young camels are calmed.

As for the words of the Most High: (bi-l-ḥaqq, with truth), al-Zamakhshari said: it is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl), or an oath, or an attribute of truthfulness. If it is a circumstantial phrase, its implied sense is: "He fulfilled the vision for him while it was connected with truth." If it is an attribute, its implied sense is: "He fulfilled it with a truthfulness connected with truth." If it is an oath, it is either an oath by Allah, for al-Ḥaqq is one of His names, or an oath by the truth which is the opposite of falsehood. This is what he said. It may also be said that there are two other aspects in it:

His words "by Allah, you will surely enter" may be an explanation of the vision, meaning: the vision was: "By Allah, you will surely enter." On this basis it becomes clear that His words ﴿Allah fulfilled﴾ were within the speech, because the vision was speech. It may also be a confirmation of the Most High's words ﴿Allah fulfilled His Messenger﴾, meaning: "By Allah, the entry will certainly occur, and the truth will certainly become manifest." So "you will surely enter" is the beginning of a sentence.

As for the Most High's words ﴿if Allah wills﴾, there are several aspects:
First: He mentioned it to teach the servants good manners and to confirm the Most High's words: ﴿And never say of anything, "I will surely do that tomorrow," without adding, "if Allah wills."﴾ [al-Kahf: 23].

Second: since the entry had not occurred in the year of al-Hudaybiyah, and the believers wished to enter and refused the peace, He said: ﴿you will surely enter﴾, but not by your strength or your will; you will enter only by the will of Allah, the Most High.

If this is the state of the promised thing in the revelation sent down, explicitly while awake, then what do you think of revelation by way of a dream, which admits of interpretation more than speech does? So if the entry was delayed, why would they mock?

The sense is: the benefit was achieved in the coming year. ﴿He knew what you did not know﴾, of the renewed benefit, ﴿and He granted, besides that, a near victory﴾, which is either the treaty of al-Hudaybiyah or the conquest of Khaybar, and we have mentioned it. **[Page 92]**

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, that He may make it prevail over all religion, and sufficient is Allah as a witness.﴾ ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. And those with him are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves. You see them bowing and prostrating, seeking bounty from Allah and His approval.﴾

This is a confirmation of the explanation of the truthfulness of Allah regarding His Messenger's vision (ru'ya). This is because, since He sent His Messenger to guide, He would not will something that does not result in guiding people, such that its opposite appears and that becomes a cause of misguidance. It may also carry a stronger meaning than that, namely that a dream which matches reality is possible for non-prophets as well, but seeing things before they occur while awake does not happen to everyone. So He said: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance﴾, and He related to him what would happen while awake. It is not far-fetched that He would show him in a dream what would take place, so there is no improbability in the truthfulness of his vision. In it there is also an explanation of the occurrence of the conquest and the entry into Makkah, through His saying: ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾. That is, one who gives it strength over the religions is not far from granting it the conquest of Makkah.

The word "guidance" (al-huda) may refer to the Qur'an, as He said: ﴿The Qur'an was sent down in it as guidance for mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185]. On this view, "the religion of truth" (din al-haqq) is what it contains of foundations (usul) and branches (furu'). It may also be that "guidance" is the miracle, meaning He sent him "with the truth", that is, "together with the truth", indicating what He legislated. It may also be that "guidance" refers to the foundations, and "the religion of truth" refers to the rulings (ahkam), because among the Messengers there were some who had no rulings but only clarified the foundations. The definite article (al-) in "al-huda" may be for totality (istighraq), meaning everything that is guidance. It may also be for a specific reference ('ahd), namely His saying: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills﴾ [az-Zumar: 23]. This may refer to the Qur'an, based on His saying: ﴿a Book whose parts resemble one another, oft-repeated, at which the skins of those who fear their Lord shiver﴾ [az-Zumar: 23], up to His saying: ﴿That is the guidance of Allah; He guides by it whom He wills﴾ [az-Zumar: 23]. Or it may refer to what all the Messengers agreed upon, based on His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah guided, so follow their guidance﴾ [al-An'am: 90]. All of these are of one category, because what is in the Qur'an agrees with what the prophets agreed upon.

His saying ﴿and the religion of truth﴾ may have several meanings:

First: "al-Haqq" is a name of Allah, the Exalted, so it is as if He said: "with guidance and the religion of Allah."

Second: "al-Haqq" is the opposite of falsehood (batil), so it is as if He said: "and the religion of the true matter."

Third: it may mean submission to the truth and adherence to it. ﴿That He may make it prevail (liyuzhirahu)﴾, that is, He sent him with guidance, which is the miracle according to one of the views. ﴿That He may make it prevail over all religion﴾, that is, over the category of religion, so that He abrogates the religions except His religion.

Most exegetes hold that the pronoun in His saying ﴿liyuzhirahu﴾ refers to the Messenger. The more apparent view is that it refers to "the religion of truth": He sent the Messenger with the true religion so that it (the religion) would prevail, that is, so that the true religion would prevail over the religions. On this view, the doer of the making-prevail may be Allah, and it may be the Prophet, that is, so that the Prophet makes the true religion prevail.

His saying ﴿and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ means: concerning the fact that he is the Messenger of Allah. This is among the things that console the hearts of the believers, for they were distressed by the disbelievers' rejection of the written treaty. They said: "We do not know that he is the Messenger of Allah, so do not write: 'Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah,' but write: 'Muhammad son of 'Abdullah.'" So He said: ﴿and sufficient is Allah as a witness﴾ concerning the fact that he is the Messenger of Allah.

In this there is a subtle meaning: although the word of Allah is sufficient in everything, it is more evidently sufficient in the matter of messengership. This is because a messenger is only such by the word of the one who sends him. So if a king says: "This is my messenger," even if everyone in the world denies that he is a messenger, their denial has no effect. Therefore He said, meaning: what defect is there in his messengership through their denial, when I confirm him as My messenger?

His saying ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ has several interpretations:

First: it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), its estimated form being: "He is Muhammad, the one previously mentioned by His saying: 'He sent His Messenger'," and "the Messenger of Allah" is an explicative apposition (atf bayan).

Second: "Muhammad" is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is "the Messenger of Allah." This is a confirmation of what came before. Because He said: ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger﴾, and his messengership depends only on his testimony, and Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, has testified to it without objection.

Third, which is derived (mustanbat): it may be said that "Muhammad" is the subject, and "the Messenger of Allah" is an explicative apposition brought for praise, not for distinguishing. ﴿And those with him﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) on "Muhammad." His saying ﴿are firm﴾ is its predicate. It is as if He, may He be exalted, said: "And those with him, all of them, are firm against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves," because the attributes of firmness and mercy are found in all of them. As for the believers, it is as in His saying: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54]. As for the Prophet (ﷺ), it is as in His saying: ﴿and be harsh with them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 73], and He said concerning him: ﴿to the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ [at-Tawbah: 128]. On this basis, His saying ﴿you see them﴾ is not addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), but is general, expressed in the form of direct address. Its estimated sense is: "O listener, whoever you are," just as we say that a preacher says, "Be attentive before attentiveness occurs," and he does not mean a specific individual.

His saying ﴿seeking bounty from Allah and His approval﴾ is to distinguish their bowing and prostration from the bowing and prostration of the disbelievers, and from the bowing and prostration of the one who shows off (murai), for he does not seek thereby that (bounty and approval). In this there is an indication of a subtle meaning: Allah, the Exalted, said of those who bow and prostrate: ﴿So He will pay them their rewards and increase them from His bounty﴾ [an-Nisa': 173]. And here He said that the one who bows seeks bounty and did not mention reward. This is because when Allah says "for you is a reward," that is from Him a favor (tafaddul). It also indicates that your deed has come in accordance with what Allah asked of you, since wages are only due for work that conforms to what the owner demanded. And the believer, when he says, "I seek Your bounty," this is from him an acknowledgment of shortcoming. So He said ﴿seeking bounty from Allah﴾ and did not say "reward."

His saying ﴿Their mark is on their faces, from the trace of prostration﴾ has two interpretations:

First: that this is on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿On the Day when some faces will be whitened﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], and He said: ﴿their light running before them﴾ [at-Tahrim: 8]. On this view we say: their light is in their faces because of their turning toward the truth, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I have turned my face toward He who originated the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-An'am: 79]. He who faces the sun has its rays fall upon his face, so light appears spread upon his face, even though the sun has an accidental light that is subject to ceasing. Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth, so whoever turns toward His face, light appears on his face that dazzles other lights.

Second: that this is in this world. On this there are two views:

The first: what is meant is what appears on the foreheads because of the abundance of prostration.

The second: what Allah, the Exalted, manifests on the faces of those who prostrate at night, of beauty by day. This is verified for one who has understanding, for two men who stay up at night: one of them is occupied with drinking and play, and the other is occupied with prayer, recitation, and seeking knowledge. On the next day, everyone distinguishes between the one who stayed up in drinking and play and the one who stayed up in remembrance and gratitude.

His saying ﴿That is their likeness in the Torah﴾ has three mentioned interpretations:

First: that "that" (dhalika) is the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿their likeness in the Torah and their likeness in the Gospel﴾ is its predicate. His saying ﴿like a seed that sends out its shoot﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "and their likeness in the Torah, and their likeness in the Gospel, is like a seed."

Second: that the predicate of "that" is His saying ﴿their likeness in the Torah﴾, and His saying ﴿and their likeness in the Gospel﴾ is a subject whose predicate is "like a seed."

Third: that "that" is a non-specific indicator, clarified by His saying ﴿like a seed﴾, as in His saying: ﴿That is the matter: that the last of these people will be cut off at dawn﴾ [al-Hijr: 66]. There is a fourth view in it: that "that" is the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimated form being: "This, which appears on their faces, is that," as one says: "the mark of a blow appeared on his face," and we say: "Indeed, by Allah, that is," meaning, "this is that apparent thing," or "the apparent thing which you are saying is that."

His saying ﴿and their likeness in the Gospel is like a seed that sends out its shoot, then strengthens it, then it becomes thick and stands upon its stalk, pleasing the farmers﴾.

That is, they were described in the two Books by this, and were likened to it. They were made like a seed because when it first emerges it is weak, and it has growth until it reaches completeness; likewise the believers. The shoot (shat') is the sprout. The word ﴿fa-azarahu﴾ may mean that it sent out the shoot and strengthened the shoot, and this is stronger and more apparent. The sentence is complete at His saying ﴿pleasing the farmers﴾.

His saying ﴿that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾: that is, Allah's causing this to grow is so that He may enrage them, or the verb that is given as the cause is ... (this is the sense).

His saying ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: that is, He promised, ﴿that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾. It is said: "Rughman li-anfika" (despite your nose), an-'ama 'alayhi (He bestowed favor upon him).

His saying ﴿forgiveness and a great reward from them﴾ is for explaining the genus, not for partitive meaning. It may be said that it is for the partitive, and its meaning: "that He may enrage the disbelievers, and for those of the disbelievers who believe, there is a great reward." The great reward and forgiveness have been mentioned many times before. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

Here is a subtle point: He, the Exalted, said regarding those who bow and prostrate that they ﴿seek bounty from Allah﴾, and He said: ﴿for them is a reward﴾, and He did not say: "for them is what they seek of that bounty." This is because the believer, at the time of the deed, did not look at his deed and did not consider it to have a reward worth counting. So he said: "I seek only Your bounty, for my deed is meager and cannot have a reward." Allah, the Exalted, gave him what He gave of bounty, and named it a reward, as an indication of the acceptance of his deed and its being placed in its proper position, and that its not being meager in the sight of Allah means the believer does not deserve a reward for it.

It has been known from what we have mentioned many times that His saying ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ explains that forgiveness is attached to faith, for every believer is forgiven, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. And the great reward is for righteous deeds. And Allah knows best.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The exegesis of this surah was completed on Thursday, the seventeenth of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three after the Prophetic Hijrah, upon its bearer be the most excellent prayers and peace. And praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and prayers and peace be upon our master Muhammad, the master of the messengers, and upon his family and all his companions.

His saying ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾: that is, He promised, ﴿that He may enrage the disbelievers by them﴾. It is said: "Rughman li-anfika" (despite your nose), an-'ama 'alayhi (He bestowed favor upon him).

His saying ﴿forgiveness and a great reward from them﴾ is for explaining the genus, not for partitive meaning. It may be said that it is for the partitive, and its meaning: "that He may enrage the disbelievers, and for those of the disbelievers who believe, there is a great reward." The great reward and forgiveness have been mentioned many times before. And Allah, the Exalted, knows best.

Here is a subtle point: He, the Exalted, said regarding those who bow and prostrate that they ﴿seek bounty from Allah﴾, and He said: ﴿for them is a reward﴾, and He did not say: "for them is what they seek of that bounty." This is because the believer, at the time of the deed, did not look at his deed and did not consider it to have a reward worth counting. So he said: "I seek only Your bounty, for my deed is meager and cannot have a reward." Allah, the Exalted, gave him what He gave of bounty, and named it a reward, as an indication of the acceptance of his deed and its being placed in its proper position, and that its not being meager in the sight of Allah means the believer does not deserve a reward for it.

It has been known from what we have mentioned many times that His saying ﴿Allah has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ explains that forgiveness is attached to faith, for every believer is forgiven, as He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that He be associated with, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. And the great reward is for righteous deeds. And Allah knows best.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The exegesis of this surah was completed on Thursday, the seventeenth of the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, in the year six hundred and three after the Prophetic Hijrah, upon its bearer be the most excellent prayers and peace. And praise is to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and prayers and peace be upon our master Muhammad, the master of the messengers, and upon his family and all his companions.
